subject: architecture
title: Data Representation
summary: How a computer turns everything into bits: number bases, integers and two's complement, bitwise tricks, IEEE 754 floating point, Unicode text, and how data is laid out in memory and on the wire.

lessons.title: Reading binary place values
lessons.summary: Each position has a weight fixed by the base.
lessons.body:
Digital computers represent numbers, text, pictures and programs using binary states. These logical states are implemented by storage and signalling hardware; there need not be one literal switch per bit. We write the two states as `0` and `1`. One binary digit is a **bit**.

Bits need an interpretation. The eight bits `01000001` can mean the number 65, the letter `A`, part of a pixel or part of an instruction. The surrounding format or program decides which meaning applies.

## Positions carry the value

In decimal, `472` means four hundreds, seven tens and two ones. Moving a digit one position left makes its contribution ten times larger. Ten is the **number base**, also called the **radix**.

Binary uses two digits, so each position is worth twice the one to its right. For an unsigned eight-bit number:

```
bit position:  7   6   5   4  3  2  1  0
weight:      128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1
```

A `1` includes that position's weight; a `0` contributes nothing. In `0000 0101`, the positions worth four and one are set, so the value is five. Moving that pattern left one place gives ten, provided the storage has room for the shifted bits.

The rightmost bit is the **least significant bit** (LSB). It decides whether an unsigned integer is odd. The leftmost is the **most significant bit** (MSB); in this unsigned interpretation it has the largest positive weight. Signed representations give it a different role, covered later.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Labelled coin trays
> Imagine trays labelled one, two, four and eight, with room for one coin in each.
>
> **How it maps:** An occupied tray contributes its labelled value, just as a set bit contributes its positional weight. The label matters as much as whether the tray is occupied.
>
> **Where it stops:** Hardware stores two logical states rather than coins. The weighting describes unsigned numbers; text and signed numbers use other interpretations.

## More bits mean more choices

Adding one bit doubles the number of possible patterns: each old pattern can now appear with a new leading zero or a new leading one. Eight bits give 256 patterns. An unsigned eight-bit field uses them for zero through 255; zero uses one of the patterns.

When designing an identifier field, count all the states it must distinguish, including any reserved values. A field with 512 patterns cannot distinguish 1,000 identifiers. Adding one bit gives 1,024 patterns and makes that possible. Changing the display from binary to decimal does not create extra capacity.

This relationship is useful when sizing a field:

```formula reference
P = 2^n
where
P: the number of distinct patterns, a dimensionless count
n: the number of independent bits
2^n: two raised to the number of bits; each additional bit doubles the count
In words: each extra bit doubles the available patterns; eight bits provide 256 distinct choices.
```

A larger range does not itself define what happens when an arithmetic result exceeds it. The integer units distinguish hardware results from language rules.

## Key takeaways
- Binary positions double in weight as you move left.
- A bit pattern needs a format or type to give it meaning.
- Each extra bit doubles capacity; reserved states reduce the usable choices.

## Further reading
- [Python integer conversion functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html)
- [NIST binary prefixes](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)

options.explanation: A set bit contributes its position weight; counting set bits alone does not give the value.

options.text: The value doubles because the set bit moves one position left
options.explanation: Correct. Each unsigned binary position is worth twice the one to its right.

options.text: The value becomes negative because a bit moved left
options.explanation: These are unsigned patterns; moving left does not introduce a sign.

options.explanation: Moving a set bit changes its positional weight, not merely the number of positions.

questions.prompt: A field has 512 available bit patterns but must distinguish 1,000 sensor identifiers. No patterns are reserved. What happens if you add one bit?

options.text: It still has too few patterns
options.explanation: An extra independent bit doubles the pattern count, making 1,024 choices.

options.text: It can distinguish every identifier, with some patterns left over
options.explanation: Correct. Every old pattern can occur with either value of the new bit, so 512 choices become 1,024.

options.text: It gains only one extra identifier
options.explanation: One bit adds a choice to every existing pattern, not just one new pattern.

options.text: It gains capacity only if displayed in hexadecimal
options.explanation: Display base changes the spelling, not the number of stored patterns.

lessons.title: Converting binary and hexadecimal
lessons.summary: Repeated division records digits from least to most significant.
lessons.body:
Hexadecimal makes long bit patterns easier to read without changing their value. Use it for memory dumps, masks and encoded fields; use decimal when the number's everyday magnitude matters.

## One hex digit represents four bits

**Hexadecimal** is base 16. Its digits run from 0 to 9, then A to F for ten through fifteen. A **nibble** is four bits, so it has exactly the sixteen patterns needed for one hex digit.

| Hex | Bits | Decimal |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0000 | 0 |
| 5 | 0101 | 5 |
| A | 1010 | 10 |
| B | 1011 | 11 |
| C | 1100 | 12 |
| F | 1111 | 15 |

Group binary digits in fours from the right. Keep four positions for each hex digit, including zeros inside the complete number:

```
1011 0101
   B    5     -> 0xB5
```

`0x` marks a hex integer literal in C and Python. Two hex digits represent an eight-bit byte. For example, bytes `C0 A8 01 0A` keep their boundaries only if the `01` and `0A` retain both digits. Dropping their zeros before joining the digits changes the value.

## Conversion changes the spelling

The same integer can be displayed in different bases:

```python
# Each conversion describes the same value.
value = 181
bin(value)       # '0b10110101'
hex(value)       # '0xb5'
int('b5', 16)    # 181
```

Hexadecimal is still positional: its rightmost position counts ones, the next counts sixteens and the next counts groups of 256. There is no special hexadecimal arithmetic inside the integer after parsing.

## Why repeated division works

To convert a non-negative integer by hand, divide by the target base and record the remainder. The remainder is the lowest digit: everything in the quotient belongs to higher positions. Repeat on the quotient, then read the recorded digits in reverse order.

For decimal 200, division by sixteen leaves twelve groups and eight left over. The eight is the low digit; twelve is written C as a single hex digit. The result is `0xC8`. Writing `0x8C` reverses the position weights.

This explains the conversion mechanism; a language's conversion functions are preferable for routine work. When inspecting a dump, preserving digit grouping and knowing the field's meaning is more useful than repeatedly calculating its decimal value.

## Key takeaways
- One hex digit represents exactly four bits.
- Keep internal zeros so bit and byte boundaries survive.
- Repeated division discovers the lowest digit first.

## Further reading
- [Python integer conversion functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html)
- [NIST binary prefixes](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)

questions.prompt: Which binary string equals `0x3C7`?

options.explanation: Correct. Each hex digit expands to exactly four bits: 3 = 0011, C = 1100, 7 = 0111.

Each hex digit must become exactly four bits. Writing the final 7 as `111` instead of `0111` loses a bit: joined up, `111100111` is 487, not 967. Only leading zeros of the whole number may be dropped.
The digits have been written in the wrong order. Hex digits keep their order; only each one is expanded.

questions.workedExample:
Expand each hex digit into four bits while preserving its position:

```
  3    C    7
0011 1100 0111
```

Only zeros at the very beginning of the complete number can be dropped without changing the value. Dropping the zero at the start of the last group shifts the earlier bits into different positions.

questions.prompt: During conversion to hexadecimal, the first division by sixteen gives remainder 8 and the final division gives remainder 12 (hex C). Which representation preserves their positional meaning?

options.explanation: The first remainder is the lowest digit; putting it first reverses the weights.
Twelve is one hexadecimal digit, C; writing 12 uses two digit positions.
Correct. The first remainder supplies the rightmost digit, and the final remainder the leftmost.

options.text: Either order works
options.explanation: The same digits in different positions generally represent different values.

questions.workedExample: Division separates the low digit from groups of sixteen. The first remainder must therefore stay on the right. Later remainders describe higher positions, giving C followed by 8.

questions.prompt: A four-byte address is shown as `C0 A8 01 0A`. A logger joins each byte's hex digits after dropping its leading zeros, producing `C0A81A`. What went wrong?

options.text: It lost byte boundaries and changed the represented value
options.explanation: Correct. Each byte needs two hex positions in this fixed-width display.

options.text: Nothing: all zero digits can be removed
options.explanation: Only leading zeros of the complete integer can be removed safely; zeros inside it hold positions.

options.text: Hexadecimal cannot represent addresses
options.explanation: Hex is a compact representation of the same address bits.

options.text: It reversed the byte order
options.explanation: The order was preserved; the widths of the last two groups were not.

lessons.title: Octal permissions and code literals
lessons.summary: Octal groups bits in threes, matching Unix permission triples.
lessons.body:
Octal is useful when a field naturally groups bits in threes. In code, choosing the wrong literal prefix can silently change a constant.

## Octal: three bits per digit

**Octal** (base 8) uses digits 0 to 7. Since 8 is 2 × 2 × 2 (2 to the power 3), each octal digit is exactly three bits. Group from the right in threes:

```
10 110 101
 2   6   5   → 0o265  (2×64 + 6×8 + 5 = 181)
```

The `0o` prefix marks octal in Python, and the octal weights are 64, 8 and 1.

Octal was popular on machines with 12-, 18- and 36-bit words, which split evenly into threes. Today you mostly meet it in **Unix file permissions**, where each digit is one `rwx` triple:

```
chmod 755 file
  7 = 111 = rwx  (owner)
  5 = 101 = r-x  (group)
  5 = 101 = r-x  (others)
```

> [!warning] The leading-zero trap in C
> An integer literal such as `010` is octal in C, C++ and Java, and in JavaScript legacy non-strict syntax. Other prefixes and floating literals have separate rules; JavaScript legacy literals containing 8 or 9 may instead be decimal. `int x = 010;` sets `x` to **8**, not 10. Zero-padding numbers to line them up in a table of constants can silently change their values. Python 3 refuses `010` with a `SyntaxError` and makes you write `0o10`.

## Bases in code

Python has built-ins for every direction:

```python
# Convert the same value between bases.
bin(181)          # '0b10110101'
hex(181)          # '0xb5'
oct(181)          # '0o265'
int('b5', 16)     # 181
int('10110101', 2)  # 181
format(181, '08b')  # '10110101'
0b1010 + 0x0F     # 25
```

In C, literals can be written as `181`, `0xB5` or `0265` (octal). `printf` prints hex with `%x` and octal with `%o`. Binary literals (`0b10110101`) and a `%b` conversion were only standardised in **C23**, though GCC and Clang accepted `0b` literals as an extension for years.

```c
/* Unsigned arguments match %x and %o. */
printf("%x %o\n", 181u, 181u);
// prints: b5 265
```

## Key takeaways
- Octal groups bits in threes, matching Unix permission triples.
- A leading zero changes a C integer literal to octal.

## Further reading
- [Python integer conversion functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html)
- [NIST binary prefixes](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)

options.explanation: This assumes `012` is decimal 12. In C a leading `0` makes the literal octal.
Correct. `012` is octal: 1 × 8 + 2 = 10, so `x + 1` is 11.
This reads `012` as hex 0x12 = 18. Hex needs the `0x` prefix; a bare leading `0` means octal.

options.text: It fails to compile
options.explanation: That is Python 3's behaviour (`SyntaxError` for `012`). C accepts it silently as octal, which is exactly why it is a trap.

questions.workedExample: The leading zero makes `012` octal in C. Its value is ten, so adding one prints `11`. The issue is the literal syntax, not the output format: `%d` prints the resulting integer in decimal. Avoid zero-padding C integer constants for visual alignment.

questions.prompt: You run `chmod 640 secrets.env`. What permissions does the file now have?

options.text: Owner `rw-`, group `r--`, others `---`
Owner `rwx`, group `r--`, others `---`
options.explanation: rwx is 7 (111). 6 is 110: read and write, but no execute.

options.text: Owner `rw-`, group `-w-`, others `---`
options.explanation: This reads 4 as the write bit. In each triple the weights are r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, so 4 is read only.

options.text: Owner `r--`, group `rw-`, others `---`
options.explanation: The digits are in the order owner, group, others, so the first digit (6) belongs to the owner.

questions.workedExample:
Each octal digit is exactly three bits, mapped to `r w x` with weights 4, 2, 1:

```
digit  bits  perms   who
  6    110   rw-     owner
  4    100   r--     group
  0    000   ---     others
```

So `ls -l` shows `-rw-r-----`. This is a common setting for a config file that a service's group needs to read but nobody else should see.

questions.prompt: In Python, `int('777', 8)` parses an octal string. What kind of value can the program then use?

options.text: A string that must stay in octal
options.explanation: Parsing produces an integer, not another string.

options.text: An integer that can only be added to other octal literals
options.explanation: The base of a literal does not create a distinct integer type.

options.text: A decimal string that loses the original value
options.explanation: The result is an integer with the same numeric value; formatting is a separate operation.

options.text: An ordinary integer, regardless of the input spelling
options.explanation: Correct. The base tells the parser how to read the text; arithmetic then works on the resulting integer.

questions.workedExample: Separate parsing from formatting. The explicit base interprets the string's digits. The result is a normal Python `int`, which can be combined with values originally written in binary, decimal or hexadecimal.

lessons.title: Finite and repeating binary fractions
lessons.summary: Fractional binary positions have weights one half, one quarter and so on.
lessons.body:
A decimal fraction can be simple to write and still need infinitely many binary digits. This matters whenever a fixed-size binary format stores measurements or prices.

## The positions continue past the point

To the right of the binary point, the positions are worth one half, one quarter, one eighth and so on. A binary `0.101` includes a half and an eighth, giving decimal 0.625. The zero skips the quarter position.

A fraction terminates in binary only when its denominator, after reducing to lowest terms, is a power of two. For example, three eighths terminates; one tenth does not, because its denominator contains a factor of five.

Decimal has its own limitation: one third repeats forever in base ten. Repetition is a property of the value and chosen base, not a fault in a particular computer.

## What a finite format must do

Binary one tenth starts `0.0001100110011...`, with a repeating tail. More bits improve the approximation but no finite number of binary fraction positions makes one tenth exact.

For a hand conversion, repeatedly double the remaining fraction. The whole-number part gives the next binary digit; continue with the fractional remainder. Reaching a zero remainder means the expansion terminates. Returning to an earlier nonzero remainder means the same digits will repeat. You do not need to carry out the whole expansion to diagnose the representability problem.

A fixed-size floating-point format must also have enough significant bits and exponent range. A terminating binary fraction can still be too large, too small or require more precision than that particular format provides.

For decimal quantities that must remain exact, choose a suitable decimal representation or integer units with an explicit rounding policy. For approximate measurements, binary floating point is often appropriate; later lessons explain its rounding and precision limits.

## Key takeaways
- Binary fraction positions successively halve in weight.
- A reduced denominator containing factors other than two gives a repeating binary expansion.
- Termination alone does not guarantee that a particular fixed-size format can store the value.

## Further reading
- [Python integer conversion functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html)
- [NIST binary prefixes](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)

questions.prompt: Which reduced fractions terminate in binary? Select all that apply.

options.text: One half
options.explanation: Correct. Its denominator is a power of two.

options.text: One tenth
options.explanation: The denominator contains a factor of five, so the binary digits repeat.

options.text: Three eighths
options.explanation: Correct. Eight is a power of two; the fraction terminates.

options.text: Three fifths
options.explanation: Five is not a power of two, so the expansion repeats.

options.text: One sixteenth
options.explanation: Correct. Repeated halving reaches this fraction exactly.

questions.workedExample: Inspect the denominators after reduction. Powers of two match binary fraction positions; a factor of five cannot be removed by adding finitely many such positions. A particular storage format must still have enough precision and range.

questions.prompt: A binary conversion of decimal one tenth returns to a nonzero fractional remainder it encountered earlier. What follows?

options.text: The same sequence of digits will repeat
options.explanation: Correct. Each step starts from the same remainder and applies the same rule, so it repeats the same next digits.

options.text: One more binary digit must make the value exact
options.explanation: A repeated nonzero remainder does not approach a terminating step.

options.text: The processor has made an arithmetic error
options.explanation: An exact conversion can repeat because the fraction has no finite binary expansion.

options.text: Using hexadecimal instead will make the finite stored bits exact
options.explanation: Changing the display does not add bits or remove the repeating binary tail.

questions.workedExample: The conversion state is its remaining fraction. Repeating that state repeats the later steps. More finite bits can improve an approximation, but cannot store one tenth exactly as a finite binary fraction.

lessons.title: Bits, words and storage units
lessons.summary: An octet is exactly eight bits; a C byte has at least eight.
lessons.body:
A size is meaningful only with its unit. Bytes, machine words and storage prefixes answer different questions, and some names depend on the platform.

## Bits, bytes and words

- **Bit**: a single 0 or 1.
- **Nibble**: 4 bits, one hex digit.
- **Byte**: today, 8 bits, the smallest addressable unit on common byte-addressed processors; some DSPs and other architectures differ. Standards documents say **octet** when they need to be unambiguous, because some historical machines used 6-, 7- or 9-bit bytes. C's `CHAR_BIT` is the number of bits in a byte (at least 8).
- **Word** (machine word): the natural unit a processor works with, usually the width of its general-purpose registers. A "64-bit CPU" usually has 64-bit general-purpose integer registers. Implemented virtual and physical address widths may be smaller and need not equal each other.

"Word" is overloaded. On x86, for historical reasons dating to the 16-bit 8086, a `WORD` is 16 bits, a `DWORD` 32 and a `QWORD` 64, even on a 64-bit chip. On ARM, a word is 32 bits. Always check which definition a document uses.

| Width | Unsigned range | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| 8 bits | 0–255 | octets; ASCII fits in seven bits |
| 16 bits | 0–65,535 | ports, UTF-16 |
| 32 bits | 0–~4.29 × 10^9 | IPv4, `int` |
| 64 bits | 0–~1.8 × 10^19 | pointers, `long long` |

### KB or KiB?

Decimal prefixes step by 1,000; binary prefixes step by 1,024. The `i` distinguishes the binary names.

| Decimal unit | Bytes | Binary unit | Bytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| kB | 1,000 | KiB | 1,024 |
| MB | 1,000,000 | MiB | 1,048,576 |
| GB | 1,000,000,000 | GiB | 1,073,741,824 |

Drive makers normally advertise decimal capacity. A drive sold as 1 TB contains a million million bytes, about 931 GiB. Counting the same bytes in larger units produces a smaller displayed number. Some software labels that binary count “GB”, which makes the difference look like missing space.

Check the unit before comparing capacities. Formatting, partitions and reserved storage can reduce usable space separately; a unit conversion alone neither removes bytes nor explains every capacity difference.

## Key takeaways
- An octet is exactly eight bits; a C byte has at least eight.
- Machine word terminology depends on the architecture.
- Decimal and binary storage prefixes count different quantities.

## Further reading
- [Python integer conversion functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html)
- [NIST binary prefixes](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)
- [Binary number — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_number)
- [Hexadecimal — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexadecimal)
- [Octal — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octal)
- [Word (computer architecture) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_(computer_architecture))
- [Binary prefix — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_prefix)
- [Built-in functions (bin, hex, int) — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html)

questions.prompt: A drive's raw capacity is unchanged, but one tool reports GB and another GiB. Why can the GiB count be smaller?

options.text: The second tool must have deleted files
options.explanation: A different unit can change the number without changing any bytes.

options.text: A GiB is smaller than a GB
options.explanation: A GiB contains more bytes, so fewer GiB cover the same capacity.

options.text: A GiB contains more bytes than a GB
options.explanation: Correct. Counting the same total with a larger unit produces a smaller number.

options.text: Binary units measure speed rather than storage
options.explanation: GiB and GB both describe amounts of data; a per-second suffix would describe a rate.

questions.workedExample: Check the units before comparing numbers. Decimal GB steps in thousands; binary GiB steps in groups of 1,024. The capacity in bytes can agree exactly even when the displayed counts differ. Partitions and reserved space are separate issues.

questions.prompt: Which statements about bytes and words are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: In x86 terminology a `WORD` is 16 bits, even on a 64-bit processor
options.explanation: Correct. The name dates from the 16-bit 8086 and was kept: `DWORD` is 32 bits and `QWORD` 64.

options.text: On ARM, a word is 32 bits
options.explanation: Correct. ARM documentation calls 16 bits a halfword, 32 bits a word and 64 bits a doubleword.

options.text: The C standard guarantees a byte is exactly 8 bits
options.explanation: C only guarantees `CHAR_BIT` is at least 8. POSIX requires exactly 8, and essentially all modern hardware uses 8, but the C standard alone does not.

options.text: A "64-bit CPU" normally means its general-purpose registers are 64 bits wide
options.explanation: Correct. Integer register width need not match implemented virtual or physical address width.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each one:

1. x86 `WORD` = 16 bits: true, a 1978 naming choice that stuck.
2. ARM word = 32 bits: true.
3. C's byte is "at least 8 bits" (`CHAR_BIT >= 8`). Some DSPs have 16- or 32-bit `char`. So the statement is false for the C standard, even though it is true in practice on PCs and phones. That is also why network standards say **octet**.
4. A 64-bit CPU normally has 64-bit general-purpose integer registers: true.

The lesson: "word" is defined by the document you are reading, so check it.

lessons.title: Why signed representations differ
lessons.summary: A bit pattern acquires meaning from its interpretation.
lessons.body:
The preceding binary units read a row of bits as a non-negative number. That is an **unsigned integer**. An unsigned field starts at zero and ends one below its pattern count, because zero uses one pattern.

So an 8-bit unsigned value runs from 0 to 255, and a 32-bit one from 0 to 4,294,967,295.

Programs also need negative numbers. There is no minus sign in hardware, only bits, so some bit patterns have to be set aside to mean negative values. Several schemes have been tried. Mainstream present-day processors use **two's complement** for signed integers. Here we compare the earlier schemes; the next units explain how two's complement uses the patterns and why it simplifies arithmetic.

## Two schemes that lost

### Sign-magnitude

The obvious idea: use the top bit as a sign (0 = positive, 1 = negative) and the rest as the size.

```
+5 = 0000 0101
-5 = 1000 0101
```

It is easy for humans to read but awkward for hardware:

- There are two zeros, `0000 0000` (+0) and `1000 0000` (−0), so equality checks need a special case.
- Adding a positive and a negative number needs different circuitry from adding two positives (you have to compare sizes and subtract).

Sign-magnitude survives in one important place: the sign bit of floating-point numbers (the floating-point units).

### Ones' complement

To negate, invert every bit:

```
+5 = 0000 0101
-5 = 1111 1010
```

Addition is nearly uniform, but you must add any carry out of the top bit back in at the bottom ("end-around carry"), and there are still two zeros (`0000 0000` and `1111 1111`). Some early machines such as the CDC 6600 used it. Today you meet it mainly in the **Internet checksum** used by IPv4, TCP and UDP, which is a ones' complement sum.

Two's complement, introduced next, has just one zero. Its top bit has a negative positional weight rather than acting as a separate sign attached to a magnitude.

## Key takeaways
- A bit pattern acquires meaning from its interpretation.
- Sign-magnitude and ones' complement have two zero patterns.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [GCC implementation-defined integers](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Integers-implementation.html)

questions.prompt: Which representation has exactly one zero bit pattern in a fixed width?

options.text: Two's complement
options.explanation: Correct. All-zero bits encode zero, and the upper half of the patterns encode strictly negative values.

options.text: Sign-magnitude
options.explanation: Sign-magnitude has positive zero and negative zero, differing in the sign bit.

options.text: Ones' complement
options.explanation: Ones' complement encodes zero as all zeros or all ones.

questions.workedExample: Compare how each scheme divides its patterns. Sign-magnitude reserves a sign plus magnitude, so a zero magnitude allows either sign. Ones' complement inverts positive zero to a second zero. Two's complement gives the top bit a negative weight and has just one zero.

lessons.title: Reading and negating two's complement
lessons.summary: The highest two's-complement bit has a negative weight.
lessons.body:
Two's complement gives negative and non-negative integers distinct patterns while keeping one representation of zero. Reading its top bit correctly explains both its range and its asymmetry.

## Two's complement

Two's complement makes one small change to the weights. The most significant bit is worth **minus** its usual weight instead of plus. All other bits keep their usual positive weights:

For 8 bits the weights are:

```
bit:      7   6   5   4  3  2  1  0
weight: -128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1
```

The pattern `1111 1011` therefore reads as −5. The lower set bits contribute 123, which is five less than the magnitude of the negative top-bit weight.

And `1000 0000` is −128 on its own, the most negative 8-bit value.

| Bits | Unsigned | Two's complement |
|---|---|---|
| 0000 0000 | 0 | 0 |
| 0111 1111 | 127 | 127 |
| 1000 0000 | 128 | −128 |
| 1111 1011 | 251 | −5 |
| 1111 1111 | 255 | −1 |

Notice that the same bit pattern means different things. `1111 1111` is 255 if you call it unsigned and −1 if you call it signed. The bits do not know; the **type** decides.

### Range

The most negative value has only the top bit set; the most positive has every bit set except the top one:

```formula reference
−2^{n−1} ≤ x ≤ 2^{n−1} − 1
where
x: a value an n-bit two's complement integer can hold
n: the number of bits
2^{n−1}: n − 1 copies of 2 multiplied together: half the number of bit patterns (128 for 8 bits)
≤: less than or equal to
In words: half of the patterns are negative and the other half are zero and the positive numbers, so the range runs from minus half the pattern count up to one less than half.
```

| Width | Min | Max |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | −128 | 127 |
| 16 | −32,768 | 32,767 |
| 32 | −2,147,483,648 | 2,147,483,647 |
| 64 | about −9.22 × 10^18 | about 9.22 × 10^18 |

The range is lopsided: there is one more negative value than positive, because zero takes one of the "non-negative" patterns. This asymmetry causes real bugs, as you will see below.

### Negating: invert and add one

To negate a value within the retained width, flip every bit and add one:

```
 +5 = 0000 0101
flip  1111 1010
 +1   1111 1011   = -5
```

For values whose negation fits, this works in both directions. Inverting pairs every bit with its opposite, giving the all-ones pattern when the two are added. Adding one to the inverted pattern makes it the additive inverse within the retained width.

For example, complementing the value five gives `1111 1010` (−6), and adding 1 gives `1111 1011`, which is −5.

A quick shortcut for doing it by hand: copy bits from the right up to and including the first `1`, then flip everything to the left of it.

> [!warning] A bit pattern is not a C overflow guarantee
> Flip-and-add-one works as an identity on the retained bits. The mathematical negation of the minimum signed value does not fit in the same signed type. Its wrapped bit pattern is unchanged; evaluating that overflowing negation in C is undefined behaviour. The later overflow unit explains the language rule.

## Key takeaways
- The highest two's-complement bit has a negative weight.
- There is one more negative value than positive.
- Flip and add one gives the negated bit pattern, subject to representability.

- [GCC implementation-defined integers](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Integers-implementation.html)

lessons.title: One adder, two integer interpretations
lessons.summary: Fixed-width hardware addition retains the low bits.
lessons.body:
Signed and unsigned addition can share the same hardware because the retained low bits follow the same wraparound rule. The type determines how to interpret those bits.

## Why two's complement won

The real prize is that **addition is the same circuit for signed and unsigned**. You add the bits, drop any carry out of the top, and the answer is correct in both interpretations (as long as it fits).

```
  1111 1011   (-5, or 251)
+ 0000 0111   ( 7)
-----------
1 0000 0010   drop the carry
  0000 0010   = 2
```

Retaining only the low bits of a fixed-width hardware result implements **modular arithmetic**: the result wraps once it runs out of bit patterns. Numbers that differ by a whole multiple of the pattern count (256 for 8 bits) end up as the same bit pattern.

Two's complement simply chooses to label the upper half of the circle as negative:

```
bits:     00 .. 7F | 80 .. FF
unsigned:  0 .. 127|128 .. 255
signed:    0 .. 127|-128 .. -1

wrap: 0x7F + 1 = 0x80
  unsigned 127 + 1 = 128  (fine)
  signed   127 + 1 = -128 (overflow)
```

To subtract, invert the second operand and add it with an incoming carry of one. This uses the same adder and implements the negation within the retained bit width.

So one adder handles `+`, `−`, signed and unsigned. For a fixed retained width, multiplication's low bits are also identical for both. Division, comparison, widening, high multiplication bits and arithmetic flags can depend on signedness.

> [!note] Now it is the law
> C23 and C++20 finally require signed integers to use two's complement. Earlier standards also allowed sign-magnitude and ones' complement, although two's complement was already the norm on common general-purpose targets. Representation does not change the rule that signed arithmetic overflow is undefined.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An odometer rolls over
> An odometer with a fixed number of wheels returns to zero after its largest reading.
>
> **How it maps:** Keeping a fixed number of result bits similarly discards complete turns through the available patterns. Signed and unsigned interpretations attach different labels to some readings.
>
> **Where it stops:** This explains retained hardware bits, not a language guarantee: signed overflow in C remains undefined.

## Key takeaways
- Fixed-width hardware addition retains the low bits.
- Signed interpretation and language overflow rules are separate questions.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [GCC implementation-defined integers](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Integers-implementation.html)

lessons.title: Widening and signed/unsigned conversions
lessons.summary: Sign extension preserves a negative signed value when widening.
lessons.body:
Widening should preserve a value, but preserving its old bits is not enough: the new upper bits must match the source interpretation.

## Sign extension

When you widen a value (a **widening conversion**), say from 8 to 32 bits, the new upper bits must preserve its value.

- **Unsigned** values are **zero-extended**: fill with 0s.
- **Signed** values are **sign-extended**: fill with copies of the sign bit.

```
-3 as 8 bits:            1111 1101
sign-extended to 16: 1111 1111 1111 1101
zero-extended to 16: 0000 0000 1111 1101
                     (= 253, wrong for -3)
```

x86 has separate instructions for each (`movsx` and `movzx`), and ARM has `sxtb` and `uxtb`. The compiler picks one based on the C type, which is why the type of a variable matters even when the bits look the same.

```c
/* The source type chooses extension. */
int8_t  s = -3;
uint8_t u = 0xFD;  /* same bits */
int32_t a = s;     /* -3  */
int32_t b = u;     /* 253 */
```

### Signed meets unsigned

When C compares a signed `int` with an `unsigned int`, the signed value is converted to unsigned first. A negative number becomes a huge positive one.

```c
/* The comparison converts x to unsigned. */
int x = -1;
unsigned y = 1;
if (x < y) puts("less");
else       puts("not less");
/* prints: not less */
```

For 32-bit unsigned int, −1 becomes 4,294,967,295, which is greater than 1. On common platforms where `size_t` does not promote to signed `int`, the same trap catches countdown loops:

```c
/* Unsafe example: the test stays true. */
/* condition cannot stop unsigned i */
for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)
    use(a[i]);
```

`i >= 0` is always true, so the condition cannot stop the loop. After unsigned wrap (or immediately when `n` is 0), indexing is out of bounds: this is undefined behaviour, not a guaranteed infinite loop. GCC warnings such as `-Wsign-compare` and `-Wtype-limits` can help; flags and diagnostics differ between compilers. A safe reverse traversal is `for (size_t i = n; i > 0; ) use(a[--i]);`.

## Key takeaways
- Sign extension preserves a negative signed value when widening.
- For int versus unsigned int, C converts the signed side to unsigned.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [GCC implementation-defined integers](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Integers-implementation.html)

lessons.title: Overflow flags and C arithmetic rules
lessons.summary: Carry and signed overflow detect different out-of-range results.
lessons.body:
A result that exceeds the available range raises two separate questions: what the instruction reports, and what the programming language permits.

## Overflow

**Integer overflow** means the true mathematical result does not fit in the type. The hardware still produces *n* bits; what those bits mean, and what your language promises, varies.

### The two flags after addition

Architectures such as x86, and flag-setting ARM add instructions, distinguish two kinds of overflow. Not all ISAs have these flags, and only instructions specified to update them do so. For a flag-setting addition:

- **Carry flag**: there was a carry out of the top bit. This means **unsigned** overflow. 200 + 100 in 8 bits gives 44 with carry set.
- **Overflow flag**: the signed result has the wrong sign. This happens only when adding two numbers of the **same** sign gives a result of the opposite sign.

```
  0110 0100  (100)
+ 0110 0100  (100)
-----------
  1100 1000  = -56 signed, 200 unsigned
```

Here the carry flag is clear (200 fits in unsigned 8 bits) but the overflow flag is set (+100 + +100 cannot be negative). Adding a positive and a negative number can never overflow.

### What C does

C treats the two cases very differently.

- Arithmetic whose resulting type is unsigned is defined to wrap around: results are reduced modulo 2 to the power of the type's width in bits (modulo 4,294,967,296 for a 32-bit `unsigned int`). Narrow unsigned operands may first promote to signed int; their expressions follow the promoted type, not an automatic wrap at the original width. `UINT_MAX + 1` is 0, and `0u - 1` is `UINT_MAX` (4,294,967,295 for 32 bits).
- **Signed overflow** is **undefined behaviour**. The C standard imposes no requirements on an execution with undefined behaviour; consequences need not be confined to the point of overflow. Optimisers may assume defined executions do not overflow.

That assumption has visible effects:

```c
/* Defined inputs cannot make this true. */
int will_overflow(int x) {
    return x + 1 < x;
}
```

You might expect this to return 1 for `INT_MAX`. GCC and Clang at `-O2` compile it to `return 0`, because for any `x` where the addition is defined, `x + 1 < x` is false. The same reasoning lets compilers widen loop counters and remove "impossible" checks, which is often good for speed and occasionally deletes a security check.

Safe alternatives:

```c
/* Detect overflow before using r. */
int r;
if (__builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &r))
    handle_error();
/* C23 standard version: */
/* #include <stdckdint.h>  */
/* if (ckd_add(&r, a, b))  */
```

Or check both directions before adding `int` operands: `if ((b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b) || (b < 0 && a < INT_MIN - b))` detects overflow without first overflowing. Compiler flags also help: GCC's `-fwrapv` specifies wrapping for signed addition, subtraction and multiplication, and `-ftrapv` requests traps for those operations; neither is a blanket fix for every undefined integer operation, and `-fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow` (UBSan) reports it at run time in testing.

### The asymmetry bug

Because the range has one extra negative value, some operations on the minimum cannot be represented:

- `-INT_MIN` should be +2,147,483,648, which does not fit. It is undefined in C; a wrapping hardware instruction may produce `INT_MIN` again, but the compiler need not preserve that result.
- `abs(INT_MIN)` is undefined for the same reason.
- `INT_MIN / -1` is undefined, and on x86 the `idiv` instruction raises a hardware exception that usually kills the process.

> [!warning] Hash bucket indices
> A classic Java bug: `Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % n`. For positive n, when the hash is `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, `Math.abs` returns it unchanged. Its remainder is negative unless n divides it exactly; a negative index throws. Use `Math.floorMod(h, n)` or mask the sign bit off.

## Key takeaways
- Carry and signed overflow detect different out-of-range results.
- Unsigned resulting types wrap; signed C overflow is undefined.
- Check before overflowing, or use checked arithmetic.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [GCC implementation-defined integers](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Integers-implementation.html)

lessons.title: Modelling fixed-width integers in Python
lessons.summary: Python integers have no fixed-width arithmetic wrap.
lessons.body:
Python integers can grow, whereas a register or protocol field has a fixed width. Modelling that boundary requires an explicit choice about which bits to keep.

## Python: no overflow, but you can fake it

Python's `int` has arbitrary precision. Arithmetic has no fixed-width wraparound, so `2**100` is exact. Storage and implementation limits still apply; a computation can fail for lack of resources. Python models a negative number as if it had an infinite row of 1s to the left, which is why bitwise operations on negatives behave like two's complement.

To see the *n*-bit pattern, or to emulate a fixed-width type, mask it:

```python
# Select eight bits, then read their sign.
def to_u8(x):
    return x & 0xFF

def to_s8(x):
    # Discard bits outside the 8-bit field.
    x &= 0xFF
    # Upper-half patterns denote negatives.
    return x - 256 if x >= 128 else x

to_u8(-3)       # 253
bin(-3 & 0xFF)  # '0b11111101'
to_s8(100+100)  # -56
to_s8(0xB5)     # -75
```

NumPy, however, uses fixed-width types, so `np.int8(100) + np.int8(100)` wraps to −56 (under the usual NumPy error settings scalar arithmetic warns, while integer array arithmetic generally wraps without that warning).

### Choose a width at the boundary

The mask in these functions is an explicit eight-bit policy. It is appropriate when modelling an eight-bit register or decoding a protocol field whose interpretation is already known. It would hide a validation failure if the application instead required rejecting values outside the permitted range.

The signed helper first discards all but the low eight bits, then interprets their top bit as a sign. Values in the upper half are reduced by the full pattern count; values in the lower half are already non-negative. This separates two decisions that a language type often packages together: which bits to retain and how to interpret those bits.

Use Python's ordinary integer arithmetic for an exact intermediate result when useful, then explicitly choose whether the external format requires rejection, saturation or wraparound. The correct boundary policy depends on the device or protocol, rather than on Python's ability to calculate a larger integer.

## Key takeaways
- Python integers have no fixed-width arithmetic wrap.
- Masking selects the low bits before signed reinterpretation.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [GCC implementation-defined integers](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Integers-implementation.html)

lessons.title: Counters and real overflow failures
lessons.summary: A finite counter needs an explicit range and rollover policy.
lessons.body:
Rollover is a system-design issue when a counter outlives assumptions made by its readers. Incident reports show why range and failure handling belong in the design.

## Design for the boundary

A fixed-width unsigned counter eventually returns to zero. Increasing its width delays that point; using finer time units makes it arrive sooner at the same width. Neither choice removes the need to define how consumers handle rollover.

For a counter using unsigned arithmetic at its specified width, subtracting the saved start value from the current value gives elapsed ticks across one rollover, provided the true elapsed interval is shorter than one complete counter period. A simple numerical comparison with a future deadline can fail when that deadline has wrapped. Longer intervals need additional state or a wider time source.

## Overflow in the real world

- **Ariane 5, 1996.** A conversion of the horizontal-bias alignment result (related to horizontal velocity) from 64-bit floating point to a 16-bit signed integer raised an exception. Both inertial reference systems failed through the same software path; the inquiry identified reuse of assumptions from Ariane 4 and inadequate protection/testing, not just a number being too large.
- **Boeing 787, 2015.** The US FAA warned that a counter in the generator control units would overflow after 248 days powered on without a restart, potentially losing all AC electrical power if the units entered failsafe together. The FAA directive states the counter-overflow interval; it does not specify a 32-bit centisecond representation. That implementation claim is omitted because it could not be verified from the directive.
> [!note] Evidence gap
> The YouTube/Gangnam Style migration anecdote is omitted: the original engineering account of counter type and migration timing was not available for reliable primary-source verification. A hypothetical signed 32-bit view counter still has the demonstrable limit 2,147,483,647.

- **The year 2038 problem.** A signed 32-bit `time_t` counting seconds from 1970 runs out at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038, and a wrapping interpretation of the next bit pattern corresponds to December 1901. Actual software may fail differently; signed overflow in C is not guaranteed to wrap. Common current 64-bit Unix ABIs use a 64-bit `time_t`, but embedded devices and old file formats remain at risk.

## Key takeaways
- A finite counter needs an explicit range and rollover policy.
- Failure reports establish causes more reliably than a plausible anecdote.

lessons.title: Bitwise operators and single-bit masks
lessons.summary: AND keeps selected bits, OR sets them and XOR toggles them.
lessons.body:
Arithmetic treats a word as one number. **Bitwise** operations treat it as a row of independent bits and work on every position at once. A 64-bit bitwise operation can manipulate up to 64 flag bits at once, which is why bitwise code appears everywhere from device drivers and network stacks to chess engines, compression and database bitmap indexes.

## The operators

| Op | C / Python | Result bit is 1 when |
|---|---|---|
| AND | `a & b` | both bits are 1 |
| OR | `a \| b` | either bit is 1 |
| XOR | `a ^ b` | the bits differ |
| NOT | `~a` | the bit was 0 |

Each operates column by column, with no carries between positions:

```
  1100 1010      1100 1010      1100 1010
& 1010 0110    | 1010 0110    ^ 1010 0110
-----------    -----------    -----------
  1000 0010      1110 1110      0110 1100
```

Three intuitions are worth memorising:

- AND with 1 **keeps** a bit; AND with 0 **clears** it.
- OR with 1 **sets** a bit; OR with 0 leaves it alone.
- XOR with 1 **flips** a bit; XOR with 0 leaves it alone.

A **bit mask** (often just called a mask) is a bit pattern whose 1s pick out the positions you care about. Choosing the operator decides what happens to those positions.

> [!warning] Bitwise is not logical
> `&&` and `||` in C (and `and` / `or` in Python) are **logical** operators. They treat each whole operand as true or false and short-circuit. `2 & 1` is 0, but `2 && 1` is 1.

## The four mask idioms

For an unsigned int `x` and a bit position `k` (from 0 up to one less than the width of `x` in bits), build the mask `1u << k`, which has a single 1 in position `k`. A wider `x` needs a correspondingly wide unsigned mask; complementing a 32-bit mask before widening it would clear the upper bits of a 64-bit x.

```c
/* Each update selects just bit k. */
x |=  (1u << k);   /* set bit k    */
x &= ~(1u << k);   /* clear bit k  */
x ^=  (1u << k);   /* toggle bit k */
if (x & (1u << k)) { /* bit is set */ }
```

Applying each one separately to `x = 0x2C` (`0010 1100`):

```
x            0010 1100
set bit 0    0010 1101   (x | 0x01)
clear bit 3  0010 0100   (x & ~0x08)
toggle bit 7 1010 1100   (x ^ 0x80)
test bit 2   0000 0100   nonzero: set
```

## Key takeaways
- AND keeps selected bits, OR sets them and XOR toggles them.
- Use an unsigned mask wide enough for the operand.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [Python bitwise integer operations](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bitwise-operations-on-integer-types)

lessons.title: Combining flags and extracting fields
lessons.summary: Not every API flag constant denotes a single independent bit.
lessons.body:
A packed word can hold independent switches, a choice between modes, or several numeric fields. Identify which kind of field you have before choosing a mask.

### Flags

Packing booleans into one integer is the most common use. POSIX `open()` takes flags OR-ed together:

```c
/* Create if absent; append each write. */
int fd = open("log.txt",
    O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_APPEND, 0644);
```

Many open options are independent bit flags, but **not every O_ constant is one bit**. Access modes are alternatives selected with O_ACCMODE; O_RDONLY is commonly zero. Test a mode with `(flags & O_ACCMODE) == O_RDONLY`, not a simple AND with O_RDONLY. Creation mode 0644 is also filtered by the process umask when a file is created. The same pattern appears in Python's `re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE` and the `enum.Flag` class.

### Extracting fields

Many formats pack several small numbers into one word. To pull one out, **shift it down, then mask it**:

```python
# Shift each colour byte into the low bits.
colour = 0x1E90FF   # RRGGBB
r = (colour >> 16) & 0xFF   # 0x1E = 30
g = (colour >> 8)  & 0xFF   # 0x90 = 144
b =  colour        & 0xFF   # 0xFF = 255
```

To pack, shift each field up and OR them together: `(r << 16) | (g << 8) | b`. CPU instruction encodings, IPv4 headers, Unix file modes and UUIDs are all decoded this way.

A mask of the low bits is one less than a power of two, because subtracting 1 from `1000...0` turns it into `0111...1`:

```formula reference
M = 2^n − 1
where
M: a mask whose low n bits are 1 and every bit above them 0; in Python it is written (1 << n) - 1
n: how many low bits the mask covers, a non-negative count
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together; written 1 << n in code
In words: a mask with consecutive low bits set keeps a field after it has been shifted down; five set low bits give the mask 31.
```

In C, the operand type, promotions and shift-count limit matter; use an appropriately wide unsigned mask and handle *n* equal to the width separately.

## Key takeaways
- Not every API flag constant denotes a single independent bit.
- Shift a field down, then mask away unrelated positions.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [Python bitwise integer operations](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bitwise-operations-on-integer-types)

Masking first keeps bits 0 to 5, which is the wrong field, then shifting throws most of it away.
`0x1F` is only 5 bits. Bits 4 to 9 inclusive is 9 − 4 + 1 = 6 bits.
You shift by the **lowest** bit position of the field, not the highest.

Masking the original low positions first would select the wrong field. If writing a live device register, check its hardware-specific access rules before assuming a read/modify/write sequence is safe.

lessons.title: Shifts, rounding and C restrictions
lessons.summary: Arithmetic right shift floors negative values; C integer division truncates.
lessons.body:
Shifts move bit positions, but signedness, rounding and language rules determine whether they can replace arithmetic safely.

## Shifts

`x << k` moves every bit *k* places left and fills with zeros. Each place doubles the value, so for unsigned values that do not lose any 1s off the top it is a multiplication by a power of two:

In bits:

```
0000 0101  (5)
<< 3
0010 1000  (40)
```

`x >> k` moves bits right, discarding the low *k* bits. What fills the top depends on the kind of shift:

- **Logical** right shift fills with 0. Used for unsigned values.
- **Arithmetic** right shift fills with copies of the sign bit, preserving the sign. Used for signed values.

```
1111 0000  (-16 signed, 240 unsigned)
logical    >> 2: 0011 1100  (60)
arithmetic >> 2: 1111 1100  (-4)
```

An arithmetic shift divides by a power of two, but it rounds **towards negative infinity**, while C's `/` rounds **towards zero**:

So on C implementations with arithmetic right shift, `-17 >> 1` is −9 while C99-and-later `-17 / 2` is −8. A compiler may implement signed division using a corrected shift, unless it proves a correction unnecessary; a bare arithmetic shift is not generally equivalent.

### The C shift rules

C leaves several cases to the implementation or makes them undefined:

- Shifting by a negative amount, or by **at least the width** of the promoted left operand, is undefined. `x << 32` on a 32-bit `int` is UB. For ordinary 32-bit x86 shifts the hardware masks the count to 5 bits (6 bits for 64-bit shifts), so it often behaves like `x << 0`, but the optimiser may do anything.
- Under C23 and earlier ISO C rules, left shift of a negative signed value is undefined, even by zero; for a non-negative signed value, the multiplied result must be representable in the promoted type. `1 << 31` with 32-bit `int` is UB; write `1u << 31`.
- Right-shifting a negative signed value is **implementation-defined**. GCC, Clang and MSVC all do an arithmetic shift.

Use suitably wide **unsigned** operands and masks, check shift counts, and account for integer promotions. A plain `1u` has unsigned-int width; use a wider constant when needed. These are C rules, not a statement of the differing modern C++ shift rules.

### Python's shifts

Python ints have no fixed width, so `1 << 100` is fine, and `>>` on negatives is always arithmetic (it floors: `-17 >> 1` is −9). `~x` is always `-x - 1`. To emulate a fixed width, mask the result: `(x << 3) & 0xFFFFFFFF`.

## Key takeaways
- Arithmetic right shift floors negative values; C integer division truncates.
- C shift counts and promoted operand types constrain validity.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [Python bitwise integer operations](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bitwise-operations-on-integer-types)

Correct. `>>` on a negative int is an arithmetic shift here, which rounds −5.25 towards negative infinity (−6). `/` truncates towards zero (−5).
C99 and later require integer `/` to truncate towards zero, so −21 / 4 is −5, not −6.

Go through the C rules for `E1 << E2` (the C standard's names: E1 is the value being shifted, E2 the shift count):

2. If the promoted E1 is signed, E1 must be non-negative and the multiplied result representable, otherwise UB. `1 << 31` gives 2³¹ > `INT_MAX`.
3. Integer promotion happens first: `uint8_t` becomes `int`. So `(uint8_t)0xFF << 24` is a signed shift whose result, 4,278,190,080, does not fit. This bites code assembling bytes into words: use `(uint32_t)b << 24`.
4. `1u << 31` is fine. `-8 >> 1` is implementation-defined, which is a weaker category: the compiler must pick and document a behaviour.

lessons.title: Reading bitwise operator precedence
lessons.summary: In C, equality binds tighter than bitwise AND.
lessons.body:
A correct mask can still produce the wrong answer if the language groups the surrounding expression differently from its author.

## Precedence traps

In C, `&`, `^` and `|` bind **more loosely** than `==`. This is a historical leftover from before C had `&&`.

```c
/* Compare the unintended / intended */
/* tests. */
if (x & 1 == 0)    /* x & (1 == 0) */
    puts("even"); /* never reached */
if ((x & 1) == 0)  /* intended test */
    puts("even");
```

Python fixed this: its bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons, so `x & 1 == 0` means `(x & 1) == 0`. Code ported between the two languages can therefore change meaning silently. Shifts also bind looser than `+` in both languages: `1 << n - 1` is `1 << (n - 1)`. When in doubt, add brackets.

### Read the expression in stages

Take the displayed C condition with an even input such as six. Equality is evaluated first: comparing one with zero produces false, represented as zero. Bitwise AND then receives the original value and zero, so its result is zero for every input. The condition therefore takes the false branch; an even number does not rescue it.

Bracketing the mask operation first instead asks whether the low bit is clear. An even input has a zero low bit, so comparing that masked result with zero succeeds. An odd input has a one low bit and fails that comparison.

Do not infer a language's precedence from a similar-looking operator in another language. When reviewing a mask test, identify the mask, bracket the extraction, and then compare with the expected masked value. Brackets explain the intended operation order to the next reader as well as to the parser.

## Key takeaways
- In C, equality binds tighter than bitwise AND.
- Use brackets to express the intended test across languages.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [Python bitwise integer operations](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bitwise-operations-on-integer-types)

options.explanation: That's what was intended, but in C `==` binds tighter than `&`, so the test is not `(x & 1) == 0`.

options.text: odd
options.explanation: Correct. It parses as `x & (1 == 0)` = `6 & 0` = 0, which is false, so the else branch runs.

options.text: Nothing; it fails to compile
options.explanation: It is valid C. Compilers warn (`-Wparentheses`), but it compiles.

options.text: Undefined behaviour
options.explanation: Every operation here is well defined. The bug is purely a precedence mistake.

2. So `x & 1 == 0` means `x & (1 == 0)`.
3. `1 == 0` is 0, so the condition is `6 & 0` = 0, false.
4. The else branch prints **odd**, for every value of x.

Fix: `if ((x & 1) == 0)`. In Python the same text works as intended, because Python's `&` binds tighter than `==`.

lessons.title: Clearing and isolating the lowest set bit
lessons.summary: Subtracting one lets AND clear the lowest set bit.
lessons.body:
Clearing one set bit at a time lets an algorithm work on the positions that matter. The useful part of these idioms is how subtraction changes the pattern.

## Classic bit tricks

The following identities assume non-negative Python integers or unsigned fixed-width C arithmetic as appropriate. Signed C `x - 1` or `-x` can overflow at the minimum value; narrow unsigned operands can also undergo integer promotion.

### Clear the lowest set bit: `x & (x - 1)`

Subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and every 0 below it into 1. AND-ing with the original clears exactly that bit:

```
x       0010 1100   (44)
x - 1   0010 1011
x&(x-1) 0010 1000   (40)
```

Uses:

- **Power-of-two test**: `x != 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0`. A power of two has exactly one bit set to 1, so clearing it leaves 0.
- **Counting bits** (Kernighan's method): repeat until zero; the number of steps is the number of 1s. It loops once per set bit, not once per position.

```python
# Clear one set bit on each iteration.
def popcount(x):
    if x < 0:
        raise ValueError("negative input")
    n = 0
    while x:
        # Remove the lowest one bit.
        x &= x - 1
        n += 1
    return n

popcount(0xB5)   # 10110101 -> 5
```

Prefer supported library/compiler operations: GCC/Clang `__builtin_popcount` (and width-appropriate variants), C23 `stdc_count_ones`, or Python 3.10+ `int.bit_count()`. They may use hardware such as x86 POPCNT or suitable ARM instructions, but lowering depends on the target. Python bit_count counts ones in the absolute value, unlike this non-negative-only loop; arbitrary-precision cost grows with integer size.

### Isolate the lowest set bit: `x & -x`

In two's complement, `-x` is `~x + 1`. That flips everything above the lowest 1 and keeps the lowest 1 itself, so AND-ing leaves only that bit:

```
x       0010 1100
-x      1101 0100
x & -x  0000 0100   (4)
```

Fenwick trees (binary indexed trees) are built on this trick. For nonzero unsigned x, the position of that bit is "count trailing zeros" (`__builtin_ctz(0x2C)` is 2). GCC's traditional `__builtin_ctz(0)` is undefined; handle zero explicitly.

## Key takeaways
- Subtracting one lets AND clear the lowest set bit.
- AND with unsigned negation isolates that bit.
- Kernighan's loop runs once per set bit.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [Python bitwise integer operations](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bitwise-operations-on-integer-types)

lessons.title: XOR identities and practical bit masks
lessons.summary: XOR cancels matching pairs and can reconstruct parity-protected data.
lessons.body:
XOR toggles the positions selected by another pattern. Applying the same toggle twice restores the original, which explains cancellation and parity.

### XOR's algebra

XOR has properties that make it unusually useful:

```formula essential
(a ⊕ k) ⊕ k = a
where
⊕: bitwise exclusive OR; a result bit is one when the input bits differ
a: the original integer bit pattern
k: the integer bit pattern used to toggle selected positions, applied twice at the same width
In words: applying the same XOR mask twice restores every original bit.
```

- A value XOR itself is 0, and XOR with 0 leaves a value alone.
- It is commutative and associative, so order does not matter.
- It is its own inverse: XOR-ing with the same key twice gets the original back.

Consequences:

- **Find the odd one out.** XOR every element of a list where every value appears twice except one. The pairs cancel and the single value is left. For a list of n fixed-width values that takes O(n) word operations (work growing in proportion to n) and O(1) auxiliary words (a fixed amount of extra memory); arbitrary-precision integer costs depend on bit length.
- **Parity.** XOR-ing all the bits gives 1 if the count of 1s is odd. RAID 5 stores the XOR of the data blocks so any one lost block can be rebuilt by XOR-ing the rest.
- **Toggle with a key.** A one-time pad XORs with a secret uniformly random message-length pad used only once. A stream cipher such as ChaCha20 XORs plaintext with a generated keystream, not directly with its short secret key. Repeating the same XOR recovers the input; that identity alone does not provide secure encryption.

```python
# Repeated values cancel, leaving 2.
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor

reduce(xor, [4, 7, 2, 7, 4])   # 2
```

The **XOR swap** (`a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;`) swaps without a temporary, but do not use it. It introduces dependencies and can lose to a plain swap, but performance depends on compilation and target. It fails for aliased a and b (the shared value becomes 0). Prefer a clear temporary or language swap; no compiler universally guarantees optimal code.

## Bitwise in the real world

- **Subnet masks.** A /24 network has mask `255.255.255.0` = `0xFFFFFF00`. A host is on the network if `(ip & mask) == (net & mask)`. Actual routing lookup uses longest-prefix matching and implementation-specific data structures. No universal throughput rate is implied.
- **Bitboards.** Chess engines such as Stockfish store each piece type as a 64-bit integer, one bit per square, and compute attacks with shifts and masks.
- **Bitmap indexes and Bloom filters.** Databases answer `WHERE a AND b` by AND-ing bitmaps of matching rows. Roaring Bitmaps (used by Lucene, Druid and others) compress them.
- **Hash tables.** For non-negative or unsigned hashes and a nonzero power-of-two table size, `hash & (size - 1)` equals `hash % size`. Compilers can already optimise remainder by a known power of two; a speedup is not guaranteed. Java's `HashMap` does this, and also XORs the hash's top 16 bits into its bottom 16 so high bits influence the bucket.
- **Permission bits.** `mode & 0o022` tests whether a file is group- or world-writable.

## Key takeaways
- XOR cancels matching pairs and can reconstruct parity-protected data.
- Remainder becomes a mask only for a nonzero power-of-two size.
- An XOR identity alone does not provide secure encryption.

## Further reading
- [C working draft N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
- [Python bitwise integer operations](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bitwise-operations-on-integer-types)
- [Bitwise operation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitwise_operation)
- [GCC bit-operation builtins](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Bit-Operation-Builtins.html)
- [Bitwise shift operators — cppreference (C)](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/operator_arithmetic)
- [Bitwise operations on integer types — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bitwise-operations-on-integer-types)
- [Bitboard — Chess Programming Wiki](https://www.chessprogramming.org/Bitboards)

lessons.title: Scientific notation and floating-point fields
lessons.summary: Normal binary values store a sign, biased exponent and fraction.
lessons.body:
Fixed-width integers are exact within a bounded range and do not directly encode fractions. Some applications need a far wider magnitude range, and measurements often include fractional values. Science, graphics and machine learning need numbers that are huge, tiny and fractional, all in a fixed number of bits.

The answer is **floating point**: scientific notation in binary. The widely used **IEEE 754** standard specifies floating-point formats and arithmetic; it was first published in 1985 and revised in 2008 and 2019. Earlier floating-point designs differed in formats and arithmetic rules. IEEE 754 improved portability, though evaluation order, formats, compiler options and language APIs can still change results.

## Scientific notation in base 2

In decimal **scientific notation** you write a number as a few digits times a power of ten:

A decimal value of 6,020 can be described as 6.02 thousands. The significant digits describe the detail; the scale describes the size.

The 6.02 is the **significand**; the **exponent** three specifies the thousands scale. The point "floats" to sit after the first digit.

Binary works the same way, with powers of two. Take 6.25:

Binary 6.25 is `110.01`. Moving its point two places left gives `1.1001`; scaling that significand up by four restores the original value.

Every non-zero binary number, once normalised, starts with `1.`. For normal values in the binary interchange formats discussed here, that leading 1 is implicit and is **not stored**. Subnormals and other formats require separate rules. This "hidden bit" gives one extra bit of precision for free.

## The layout

A number is stored as three fields:

```
float (binary32):
 1 bit   8 bits      23 bits
[sign][ exponent ][  fraction  ]

double (binary64):
 1 bit  11 bits      52 bits
```

The value of a normal value can also be reconstructed using this reference relationship. Zero, subnormals, infinities and NaNs need their own rules:

```formula reference
v = (−1)^s (1.f) 2^{e − bias}
where
v: the value the bits represent
s: the sign bit: 0 for positive, 1 for negative
(−1)^s: −1 to the power s: 1 when s = 0 and −1 when s = 1, so it only sets the sign
1.f: the significand: a 1, then the binary point, then the stored fraction bits f; the leading 1 is not stored (the hidden bit)
f: the fraction field: the bits after the binary point, 23 bits in a float and 52 in a double
e: the exponent field, read as an unsigned whole number (8 bits in a float, so 0 to 255)
bias: a fixed number subtracted from e to get the true exponent: 127 for float, 1023 for double, 15 for half; for an exponent field of k bits it is 2 to the power (k − 1), minus 1
2^{e − bias}: 2 to the power of the true exponent; it slides the binary point left or right
In words: for a normal value, restore the leading one, scale the significand using the stored exponent after removing its bias, then apply the sign bit.
```

The sizes of the fields and the bias for each common format:

| Format | Exp bits | Fraction bits | Bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| half (binary16) | 5 | 10 | 15 |
| float (binary32) | 8 | 23 | 127 |
| double (binary64) | 11 | 52 | 1023 |

### Why a bias?

The exponent must be able to go negative (for numbers below 1). Rather than using two's complement for negative exponents, these IEEE formats add a fixed bias before storing the exponent as an unsigned number. For binary32, a true exponent of two is stored as 129; a true exponent of minus three is stored as 124. Decoding subtracts the bias to recover the scale.

The all-zero and all-one exponent fields have special meanings. For normal binary32 values, stored exponents run from 1 through 254 and true exponents from −126 through +127.

The payoff: for positive floats, a larger bit pattern means a larger number. Unsigned ordering of the canonical binary32/binary64 encodings agrees with numeric ordering for values with sign bit zero, excluding NaNs. Negative zero, negative numbers and NaNs require additional handling.

The sign is a separate bit, so floats are **sign-magnitude**: changing the sign of a binary32 value flips bit 31 (bit 63 for binary64).

## Key takeaways
- Normal binary values store a sign, biased exponent and fraction.
- The implicit leading one increases normal-value precision.

## Further reading
- [Oracle numerical computation guide](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_math.html)
- [Python floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)

lessons.title: Encoding and decoding binary32
lessons.summary: Normalise the binary significand before applying the exponent bias.
lessons.body:
A binary32 decoder must identify the fields before doing arithmetic. The sign occupies one bit, the exponent eight bits, and the stored fraction 23 bits. Normal values use exponent bias 127 and an implicit leading one; reserved exponents select different rules.

## Read the fields, then the value

Here is the encoding of −6.25:

```
sign  exponent  fraction
1     10000001  10010000000000000000000
```

- The sign bit says negative.
- Stored exponent 129 means a true exponent of two after removing the bias: scale the significand by four.
- Fraction bits start `1001`. Restore the implicit leading one to get binary `1.1001`, whose value is 1.5625.

Together these fields represent −6.25. The complete encoding is `0xC0C80000`. The sign does not participate in two's-complement negation: flipping that one sign bit gives positive 6.25 while keeping the exponent and fraction.

## Use a decoder to inspect bytes

Python's `struct` module can encode and decode the format directly:

```python
# Explicit big-endian IEEE binary32 bytes.
import struct
struct.pack('>f', -6.25).hex()
# 'c0c80000'
raw = bytes.fromhex('41580000')
struct.unpack('>f', raw)
# (13.5,)
```

The `>` chooses big-endian byte order, and `f` chooses binary32. A hex value from a debugger and a sequence of bytes are not interchangeable without knowing byte order. The later memory-layout units explain that distinction.

## Diagnose a decoding mistake

A decoder that reads the fraction as an integer loses its fractional position weights. A decoder that omits the hidden one makes normal magnitudes too small. A decoder that treats the stored exponent as the true exponent applies a wildly incorrect scale.

Classify the exponent first. With an all-zero exponent, zero and subnormal rules apply; with an all-one exponent, infinity and NaN rules apply. The normal rule cannot decode every bit pattern.

When writing an encoder, first express the magnitude with the binary point after its leading one, record the scale, and store the remaining fraction bits. If they do not fit, rounding is required. Use a tested format implementation for routine conversion; the important skill is recognising which field caused a wrong result.

## Key takeaways
- Decode the field roles before interpreting the value.
- Normal values restore a hidden one and remove the exponent bias.
- Check reserved exponents and byte order before applying the normal rule.

## Further reading
- [Oracle numerical computation guide](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_math.html)
- [Python floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)

lessons.title: Decimal fractions and nearest-even rounding
lessons.summary: A finite binary format rounds repeating decimal fractions.
lessons.body:
Rounding happens when a value enters a finite binary format and can happen again after each arithmetic operation. A short decimal spelling does not guarantee an exact binary value.

## Why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3

The binary-fraction unit showed that 0.1 in binary is `0.000110011001100...`, repeating forever. A binary32 value has only 24 significant bits, so storing one tenth requires rounding. Its stored value is slightly above one tenth; binary64 gives a closer approximation but is still inexact.

On the usual Python platform using IEEE binary64 and nearest-even rounding, each of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 is rounded to a nearby representable value. Adding the first two rounds again, and that result differs from the stored 0.3:

```python
# Observe rounded binary64 arithmetic.
>>> 0.1 + 0.2
0.30000000000000004
>>> 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
False
```

This is not a bug in Python, or JavaScript, or your CPU. It is the correct IEEE 754 result: the sum of the two nearest doubles, rounded to the nearest double, which happens to be the one just above 0.3's nearest double.

## Rounding

IEEE 754's default rounding mode is **round to nearest, ties to even**. When a result is exactly halfway between two representable values, it picks the one whose last bit is 0. This avoids the upward bias of always rounding halves up.

Python's `round()` uses the same rule for halfway cases: `round(0.5)` is 0, `round(1.5)` is 2, `round(2.5)` is 2. But `round(2.675, 2)` gives 2.67, not because of ties-to-even, but because the stored binary value is slightly below decimal 2.675, so this is not an exact halfway case.

## Key takeaways
- A finite binary format rounds repeating decimal fractions.
- Nearest-even resolves halfway cases using the last retained bit.

## Further reading
- [Oracle numerical computation guide](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_math.html)
- [Python floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)

lessons.title: Precision, spacing and lost increments
lessons.summary: Spacing doubles between successive normal binades.
lessons.body:
Assume nearest-even binary32 or binary64 arithmetic: halfway results go to the representable value whose last retained bit is zero.

## Precision and range

The significand has a fixed number of bits, so the **gap between neighbouring floats grows** with their size. Floats are dense near zero and sparse far away.

The table uses scientific notation: the e suffix introduces a decimal exponent. For example, an exponent of negative seven scales the preceding digits by one ten-millionth.

| | float | double |
|---|---|---|
| Significant bits | 24 | 53 |
| Decimal digits | about 7 | about 15–16 |
| Machine epsilon | about 1.19e−7 | about 2.22e−16 |
| Largest | ≈ 3.40e38 | ≈ 1.80e308 |
| Consecutive exact integers through | 16,777,216 | 9,007,199,254,740,992 |

**Machine epsilon** is the gap between 1.0 and the next float above it. More significant bits make that gap smaller. It is a precision measure near one, not a universal absolute error tolerance.

For normal finite values with a next finite neighbour further from zero, the gap scales with the size of the number. It is constant within each **binade** (the range from one power of two up to the next) and doubles at each power of two:

```formula reference
Δ = 2^E ε   for 2^E ≤ |x| < 2^{E+1}
where
Δ: delta, the gap between x and the next representable value further from zero
x: a normal floating-point value with a next finite neighbour further from zero
|x|: the absolute value of x: x without its sign
E: the true exponent of x: the power of two at or just below |x|
ε: machine epsilon, 2^{−23} for float and 2^{−52} for double
≤: less than or equal to; <: less than
In words: normal floating-point spacing is constant between successive powers of two and doubles in the next such interval. Near 16,777,216, binary32 values are two apart.
```

Subnormals have fixed absolute spacing. Two consequences:

- Above 16,777,216 a binary32 value cannot represent every integer. `16777217.0f` rounds to 16,777,216. Using a `float` for a counter or a timestamp silently stops counting.
- Above 9,007,199,254,740,992 a double cannot either. That is why JavaScript Number values (binary64, distinct from BigInt) have `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, one less than that boundary (9,007,199,254,740,991); decimal strings or BigInt are alternatives for larger exact integer IDs.

Adding a small number to a big one can lose it entirely:

```python
# The unit increment rounds away first.
>>> 1e16 + 1.0 - 1e16
0.0
```

Near ten thousand million million, neighbouring binary64 values are two apart.

Adding one to ten thousand million million is exactly halfway between two doubles, and nearest-even rounds back to the starting value.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A map at different scales
> A ruler on a local map distinguishes small distances; the same marks on a world map cover much larger distances.
>
> **How it maps:** A fixed number of significand bits supplies a fixed amount of detail while the exponent changes the scale. At larger magnitudes, adjacent representable values are further apart.
>
> **Where it stops:** Normal floats change spacing in power-of-two intervals; subnormals have fixed spacing. This is a representation limit, not uncertainty in the original measurement.

## Key takeaways
- Spacing doubles between successive normal binades.
- A large floating counter can stop responding to unit increments.
- Small additions can disappear before later subtraction.

## Further reading
- [Oracle numerical computation guide](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_math.html)
- [Python floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)
