lessons.title: Zeros, infinities and NaNs
lessons.summary: Reserved exponent fields encode zeros, subnormals, infinities and NaNs.
lessons.body:
Some floating-point bit patterns represent exceptional states instead of ordinary finite magnitudes. Classifying these states helps diagnose failed calculations.

## Special values

The all-zeros and all-ones exponents are reserved:

| Exponent | Fraction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| all 0s | 0 | ±0 |
| all 0s | non-zero | subnormal |
| all 1s | 0 | ±infinity |
| all 1s | non-zero | NaN |

So a float's normal exponent range is 1 to 254 (true exponent −126 to +127). The largest finite value has the biggest normal exponent and every fraction bit set:

The largest finite binary32 value is about 3.40 × 10^38, and binary64 reaches about 1.80 × 10^308. A mathematical result just above the maximum can still round back to it; a sufficiently large result rounds to infinity in nearest-even mode.

### Signed zero

+0 (`0x00000000`) and −0 (`0x80000000`) compare equal, but they have different encodings and retain different signs. Under IEEE 754 non-trapping arithmetic, `1 / -0.0` is −infinity. C requires an implementation providing the relevant IEC 60559/Annex F behaviour; plain ISO C does not universally promise this result. They record which side of zero a tiny result underflowed from, which matters in complex arithmetic and some physics code.

### Infinity

Under the usual non-trapping round-to-nearest mode, overflow produces ±infinity rather than integer-style wrapping; directed rounding modes may instead return a largest finite value. For example, `1e308 * 10` is `inf`. IEEE 754 non-trapping division gives +infinity for `1.0 / 0.0`; C implementations following Annex F provide that behaviour. Python instead raises `ZeroDivisionError`. Integer division by zero in C is undefined. Infinity behaves sensibly: `inf + 1 == inf`, `1 / inf == 0`.

### NaN

**NaN** (not a number) is the result of invalid operations: `0.0 / 0.0`, `inf - inf`, `sqrt(-1.0)`. NaN propagates through ordinary operations such as addition and multiplication, often contaminating a calculation. Some functions have specified exceptions: Python `math.pow(float("nan"), 0.0)` returns 1.0. Python also raises exceptions for operations such as `0.0 / 0.0` and `math.sqrt(-1.0)` instead of returning NaN.

NaN is **unequal to everything, including itself**. for ordinary floating-point values, `x != x` is true only for NaN, which is the traditional test. Use `math.isnan(x)` in Python and `isnan(x)` in C. NaNs do not supply an ordinary total numeric ordering, so a sort using plain numeric comparisons may not give the ordering you intended. Choose explicitly where NaNs should go.

## Key takeaways
- Reserved exponent fields encode zeros, subnormals, infinities and NaNs.
- Language error handling can differ from non-trapping IEEE arithmetic.
- NaN compares unequal to itself.

## Further reading
- [Oracle numerical computation guide](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_math.html)
- [Python floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)

Prefer `math.isnan(x)` for readability. Beware: Python's `list.__contains__` checks identity first, so `x in [x]` is `True` even though `x == x` is `False`.

lessons.title: Subnormals and gradual underflow
lessons.summary: A zero hidden bit extends the range towards zero with fixed spacing.
lessons.body:
Subnormals keep small nonzero results representable after the normal exponent range runs out. They trade significant precision for a gradual approach to zero.

### Subnormals

Without special handling, the smallest positive float would be 1.0 × 2^−126 ≈ 1.18 × 10^−38, and there would be a gap down to 0. **Subnormal** (denormal) numbers fill it. With exponent field 0, the hidden bit becomes 0 and the exponent is fixed at −126:

```formula reference
v = (−1)^s (0.f) 2^{−126}
v_min = 2^{−149}
where
v: the value of a subnormal float
s: the sign bit
0.f: the significand with a leading 0 instead of the hidden 1, then the 23 stored fraction bits f
f: the fraction field
v_min: the smallest positive subnormal float: only the last fraction bit set
2^{−126}: the fixed scale for subnormal floats, the same as the smallest normal exponent
In words: subnormals give up the hidden 1 to keep counting down in equal steps, reaching about 1.4 × 10^−45 before zero.
```

The smallest positive subnormal has only the last fraction bit set and is about 1.4 × 10^−45. The spacing stays fixed as values approach zero, so the number of useful significant bits decreases. An all-zero fraction represents zero instead.

With gradual underflow and correctly rounded subtraction of finite inputs in the same format, distinct representable numbers do not collapse to zero merely because their difference is tiny. Some processors and operations incur costly assists for subnormal operands or results; others handle them efficiently. FTZ and DAZ modes change arithmetic semantics by flushing small results or treating small inputs as zero, so enable them only when the application tolerates that change.

## Key takeaways
- A zero hidden bit extends the range towards zero with fixed spacing.
- Flush-to-zero modes change numerical results.

## Further reading
- [Oracle numerical computation guide](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_math.html)
- [Python floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)

options.explanation: A normal value needs a nonzero exponent field and the implicit leading one.

options.text: The smallest positive subnormal value
options.explanation: Correct. The zero hidden bit and lowest fraction bit encode the smallest positive subnormal.

options.text: Positive zero
options.explanation: Zero needs an all-zero fraction as well as an all-zero exponent.

questions.workedExample: The exponent field selects the subnormal rule. Its hidden bit is zero, but the fraction is nonzero, so this is not zero. With only the lowest fraction position set, no smaller positive nonzero pattern exists in binary32.

lessons.title: Numerical safeguards and smaller floats
lessons.summary: Use tolerances justified by the application and exact decimal or integer money values.
lessons.body:
Choose a numeric representation and error policy for the application. More bits help only when they address the actual failure: range, precision or an exactness requirement.

## Real-world failures and fixes

> [!example] The Patriot missile, 1991
> The GAO investigation found that limited precision in a time conversion caused an increasingly inaccurate tracking calculation. After over 100 hours of continuous operation, the system looked in the wrong place for the incoming Scud, which hit barracks and killed 28 Americans. This was an accumulated numerical conversion error, not physical clock drift or a failure of IEEE binary32 specifically. The GAO reports a roughly 0.34-second time error at 100 hours.

Practical rules:

- **Choose equality semantics for the problem.** Exact equality is appropriate for some exact/discrete computations. For approximate results use justified relative and absolute tolerances; near zero, a positive abs_tol may be needed. `math.isclose` does not choose a scientifically valid error allowance for you.
- **Do not store money in floats.** Use integer minor units (pence, cents) or a decimal type such as Python's `decimal.Decimal` or SQL's `NUMERIC`.
- **Order of operations matters.** Float addition is not associative: `(0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3` is 0.6000000000000001, but `0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3)` is 0.6. Parallel reductions on GPUs can give slightly different answers from run to run for this reason.
- **Summing many values** can accumulate rounding error. Compensated summation and math.fsum reduce it; they do not make every result exact or eliminate all overflow and platform effects. Since Python 3.12, the built-in `sum()` also uses compensated summation for floats, so `sum([0.1] * 10)` is 1.0, while a plain `+=` loop gives 0.9999999999999999.
- **Avoid subtracting nearly equal numbers** when you can rearrange the formula. Cancellation can expose error already present in approximate operands and produce a large relative error. Subtraction of nearby floating-point values can itself be exact; rearrangement is useful when it improves the conditioning or avoids prior errors.

## Smaller floats for machine learning

Many neural-network workloads can use reduced precision with suitable training and accumulation strategies. Halving element size halves storage for the same tensor, not necessarily total model memory or traffic: auxiliary states and wider accumulators remain. Two common 16-bit formats are:

| Format | Sign/Exp/Frac | Max |
|---|---|---|
| FP16 (half) | 1 / 5 / 10 | 65,504 |
| bfloat16 | 1 / 8 / 7 | ≈ 3.39e38 |

The exponent controls the broad range while fraction bits control precision. A wider exponent can keep large activations finite, but fewer fraction bits mean coarser rounding.

**bfloat16**, used by Google TPUs, has the same sign and exponent widths as float32 but a shorter fraction. Conversion normally rounds rather than simply discarding bits. Its normal exponent range matches float32, with slightly different finite limits. Subnormal handling depends on the implementation: Cloud TPU conversion flushes bfloat16 subnormals to zero. FP16 has more precision but a maximum of 65,504. Loss scaling helps prevent small gradients from underflowing; it does not fix activations that exceed FP16's maximum. Recent GPUs go further with 8-bit and even 4-bit floating-point formats.

## Key takeaways
- Use tolerances justified by the application and exact decimal or integer money values.
- Summation order can affect rounded results.
- FP16 and bfloat16 trade precision and exponent range differently.

## Further reading
- [Oracle numerical computation guide](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_math.html)
- [Python floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)
- [IEEE 754 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754)
- [Single-precision floating-point format — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-precision_floating-point_format)
- [What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic — David Goldberg](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html)
- [Floating-point arithmetic: issues and limitations — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html)
- [Float Toy — interactive bit editor](https://evanw.github.io/float-toy/)
- [Bfloat16 floating-point format — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bfloat16_floating-point_format)

- [GAO investigation of the Dhahran Patriot failure](https://www.gao.gov/assets/imtec-92-26.pdf)
- [Python math accuracy and isclose](https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html)
- [Google TPU bfloat16 semantics](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/bfloat16)

questions.prompt: An invoicing service totals line items with `total += price` using Python floats. A customer buys ten items at £0.10, and a check `total == 1.00` fails. What is the best fix?

options.text: Round `total` to 2 decimal places before every comparison
options.explanation: That hides this symptom but leaves errors in stored totals, tax calculations and sums of thousands of lines, and rounding floats has its own surprises (`round(2.675, 2)` is 2.67).

options.text: Switch from float to a 128-bit float type
options.explanation: More bits reduce the error but cannot remove it: 0.10 is still a repeating binary fraction at any width.

options.text: Store amounts as integer pence (or use `decimal.Decimal`)
options.explanation: Correct for amounts in specified minor units, or decimal arithmetic with a specified precision and rounding policy. Tax, currency conversion and fractions of a minor unit still require explicit rounding rules.

options.text: Use `sum()` instead of a loop, which fixes it permanently
options.explanation: Since Python 3.12 `sum()` uses compensated summation, so this example gives 1.0, but the individual amounts are still inexact and later arithmetic (tax, discounts) can still drift.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each £0.10 is stored as 0.1000000000000000055511...
2. Ten `+=` steps, each rounded, give `0.9999999999999999`.
3. `0.9999999999999999 == 1.0` is False.

With integer pence:

```python
total = 0
for _ in range(10):
    # Keep the total in integer pence.
    total += 10      # pence
total == 100         # True
```

Or `Decimal('0.10') * 10 == Decimal('1.00')`, which is True. Note `Decimal(0.1)` from a float would copy the error; build Decimals from strings.

questions.prompt: Which statements about IEEE 754 doubles are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: `x != x` is true only when x is NaN
options.explanation: Correct. Every other value, including infinities and both zeros, equals itself.

options.text: `0.0 == -0.0` is true, even though their bit patterns differ
options.explanation: Correct. +0 is all zeros and −0 has only the sign bit set, but the standard says they compare equal.

options.text: Subnormal arithmetic can incur substantial extra cost on some processors and operations
options.explanation: Correct. Expensive assists are implementation-dependent; FTZ/DAZ may avoid them by changing results, not by preserving full gradual-underflow semantics.

options.text: IEEE 754 non-trapping floating-point division must crash on 1.0 / 0.0
options.explanation: False. IEEE non-trapping division returns positive infinity and raises a status flag. Language APIs can differ: Python raises ZeroDivisionError, and C requires the relevant IEC 60559/Annex F support for this guarantee.

options.text: Float addition is associative, so `(a + b) + c == a + (b + c)`
options.explanation: Each addition rounds, so grouping changes the result: `(0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3` is 0.6000000000000001 but `0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3)` is 0.6.

questions.workedExample:
1. For IEEE floating values, x != x detects NaN.
2. Signed zeros compare equal while retaining different sign bits.
3. Subnormal performance depends on the processor and operation; some incur expensive assists.
4. IEEE non-trapping 1.0 / 0.0 returns infinity, but languages can define an exception instead. Plain ISO C does not guarantee Annex F behaviour on every implementation.
5. Rounded addition is not associative; changing grouping can change the result.

questions.prompt: You switch a neural network's training from float32 to 16-bit floats to save memory. With FP16, some activations exceed 70,000 and become infinity, and training diverges. Which change most directly expands the representable range for these activations while staying at 16 bits?

options.text: Use bfloat16, whose 8-bit exponent gives a much larger finite range than FP16
options.explanation: Correct. bfloat16 has a finite range close to float32's, so values around 70,000 remain finite, though they are rounded because precision is limited.

options.text: Use FP16 with subnormals enabled
options.explanation: Subnormals extend the range near **zero**, not at the top. FP16's maximum is still 65,504.

options.text: Use a 16-bit integer instead
options.explanation: `int16` maxes out at 32,767, which is worse, and loses all fractional precision.

options.text: Switch to round-towards-zero mode
options.explanation: Toward-zero rounding can avoid an infinity by returning a largest finite value, but it still cannot represent 70,000 faithfully. It does not solve the inadequate range.

questions.workedExample: FP16's finite maximum is 65,504, so the stipulated activations exceed its range. bfloat16 allocates more bits to the exponent and fewer to the fraction, keeping values around 70,000 finite with coarser precision. Subnormals help near zero, not at the maximum. Loss scaling addresses small gradients; overflow-prone forward operations may need rescaling or a wider format.

lessons.title: ASCII, Unicode and scalar values
lessons.summary: A character set and its byte encoding answer different questions.
lessons.body:
Text is just numbers with an agreed mapping. The letter `A` is stored as 65 because, long ago, people agreed that 65 means `A`. The hard part is that for decades different groups agreed on different mappings, and a byte written under one was read under another.

This lesson separates two ideas that are easy to blur:

- A coded **character set** assigns numbers to its encoded elements; a user-perceived character can require several of those elements. In Unicode that number is a **code point**.
- A **character encoding** turns those numbers into bytes. UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 are three encoding forms for Unicode scalar values (code points excluding U+D800 through U+DFFF, the surrogate range). UTF-16 and UTF-32 also need a byte-order convention for byte serialisation.

## ASCII and the code-page era

**ASCII** uses 7 bits for 128 code positions. Its early revisions differed; the established table preserved by Unicode contains control codes 0–31 and 127, then space, digits, punctuation, and upper- and lower-case English letters.

```
'0' = 0x30   'A' = 0x41   'a' = 0x61
```

Two tidy design choices are worth knowing. First, the ten digit characters are numbered in order, starting at 0x30. After checking that a character is an ASCII digit, subtract the code of `'0'` to obtain its numeric value. The character `'7'` is a text code, not the integer seven.

That is why `c - '0'` in C converts a digit character to its value. Second, upper- and lower-case ASCII letters differ only in bit 5. Setting that bit changes uppercase to the corresponding lowercase letter. This depends on the ASCII layout; it is not a Unicode case-conversion algorithm.

So `c | 0x20` can lower-case an ASCII letter, but must not be applied indiscriminately to punctuation or UTF-8 bytes.

In an eight-bit byte, seven-bit ASCII leaves the top 128 values unused. Everyone filled them differently: ISO 8859-1 (Latin-1) for Western Europe, Windows-1252 (mostly shares Latin-1 assignments but replaces many C1-control positions with other characters), KOI8-R for Russian, Shift JIS for Japanese, and many others. Plain text bytes often lack encoding metadata, though a file format can include such metadata. Shift JIS is variable-width, not merely a different assignment of single high bytes. Open a Russian file with the Western code page and you got gibberish, which the Japanese call **mojibake**.

## Unicode: code points and scalar values

**Unicode** provides a shared repertoire of encoded characters across many writing systems, written `U+` followed by hex:

```
U+0041  A    LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A
U+00E9  é    LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE
U+20AC  €    EURO SIGN
U+4F60  你   CJK UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH
U+1F600 😀   GRINNING FACE
```

The code space runs from U+0000 to **U+10FFFF**, which is 1,114,112 positions in 17 **Unicode planes** of 65,536.

Plane 0, the **Basic Multilingual Plane** (BMP, U+0000 to U+FFFF), includes many common scripts. Supplementary planes contain further scripts, CJK characters and many emoji; some emoji are in the BMP. Not every code point is an assigned character: the code space also includes surrogates, private-use areas, noncharacters and unassigned positions.

The first 128 code points are identical to ASCII, and the first 256 to Latin-1.

## UTF-32: simple and wasteful

UTF-32 stores each Unicode scalar value as one 32-bit code unit. That is four octets per scalar value, so finding the code point at any position takes O(1) time: the same small amount of work whatever the position, because each successive scalar value starts four octets after the previous one, counting from the first encoded scalar value. But English text becomes four times larger, and the bytes depend on endianness (UTF-32LE vs UTF-32BE). It is used internally sometimes, rarely for storage or exchange.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Catalogue numbers and shipping labels
> A catalogue assigns each item a number; a shipping system decides how that number appears on a label.
>
> **How it maps:** Unicode code points identify encoded elements, while Unicode encodings specify the code units or bytes used to carry scalar values.
>
> **Where it stops:** One user-perceived character can involve several code points; a code point does not imply a fixed number of bytes.

## Key takeaways
- A character set and its byte encoding answer different questions.
- Unicode scalar values exclude surrogate code points.
- UTF-32 uses one four-octet unit per scalar value.

## Further reading
- [Unicode 17 conformance and encoding forms](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode17.0.0/core-spec/chapter-3/)
- [RFC 3629: UTF-8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629)

questions.prompt: Which Unicode code point is excluded from the scalar values encoded by well-formed UTF-8?

options.explanation: U+0000 is a scalar value and encodes as a zero byte; C string conventions are a separate limitation.

options.text: U+10FFFF
options.explanation: U+10FFFF is a scalar value even though it is a noncharacter; noncharacters are not surrogate code points.
Correct. U+D800 is in the reserved surrogate range, excluded from Unicode scalar values.

questions.workedExample: Begin with the Unicode code space, from U+0000 through U+10FFFF. Remove the surrogate range U+D800 through U+DFFF to obtain scalar values. This excludes U+D800 while retaining both endpoints of the code space. A protocol may impose additional restrictions, but that does not change the scalar-value definition.

lessons.title: Encoding and recognising UTF-8
lessons.summary: UTF-8 uses one to four bytes per scalar value.
lessons.body:
UTF-8 carries both character data and byte-boundary markers. Recognising those markers explains variable length, ASCII compatibility and strict validation.

## UTF-8: the encoding that won

**UTF-8** was designed by Ken Thompson and Rob Pike in 1992. It uses 1 to 4 bytes per Unicode scalar value:

| Code points | Bytes | Bit pattern |
|---|---|---|
| U+0000–007F | 1 | `0xxxxxxx` |
| U+0080–07FF | 2 | `110xxxxx 10xxxxxx` |
| U+0800–FFFF, excluding D800–DFFF | 3 | `1110xxxx` + 2 × `10xxxxxx` |
| U+10000–10FFFF | 4 | `11110xxx` + 3 × `10xxxxxx` |

The `x` positions carry the code point's bits, most significant first. For a valid multibyte sequence, the number of leading 1s gives the **total** byte count, not the number of following bytes, and every continuation byte starts with `10`.

Only the shortest encoding of a scalar value is valid. The byte markers alone do not establish validity: surrogates, values above U+10FFFF and non-shortest forms must be rejected or handled under the decoder's specified error policy.

### Worked example: € (U+20AC)

U+20AC is between 0x0800 and 0xFFFF, so it needs 3 bytes with 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 payload bits.

```
0x20AC = 0010 0000 1010 1100

split 4 | 6 | 6:
0010 | 000010 | 101100

fill the template:
1110 0010  10 000010  10 101100
= E2       82         AC
```

So `€` is the three bytes `E2 82 AC`.

### Worked example: 😀 (U+1F600)

Above U+FFFF, so 4 bytes with 3 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 21 payload bits.

```
0x1F600 as 21 bits:
000 011111 011000 000000

11110 000 = F0
10 011111 = 9F
10 011000 = 98
10 000000 = 80
```

`😀` is `F0 9F 98 80`.

```python
# Encode code points into UTF-8 bytes.
'€'.encode('utf-8')   # b'\xe2\x82\xac'
'😀'.encode('utf-8')  # b'\xf0\x9f\x98\x80'
```

### Why UTF-8 is so good

- **ASCII compatible.** ASCII text is valid UTF-8 byte for byte. Tools that recognise only ASCII delimiters can often process UTF-8 unchanged, provided they otherwise preserve arbitrary bytes.
- **No zero bytes** except for U+0000 itself, so C strings and `strlen` still function (counting bytes, not characters).
- **Self-synchronising.** In a valid UTF-8 stream, continuation bytes start with 10 and other bytes start a sequence. At most three continuation bytes remain after an arbitrary position inside a character. Invalid bytes such as C0, C1 and F5–FF require rejection or specified error handling; corruption is not guaranteed to damage exactly one character.
- **No byte order.** It is a sequence of bytes, so endianness never arises.
- **Sorting.** Lexicographic comparison of unsigned bytes in valid UTF-8 agrees with scalar-value order. This is not linguistic collation, and normalisation differences still matter.

UTF-8 is widely used for interchange. RFC 8259 requires it for JSON exchanged outside a closed ecosystem; Rust and Go source text use UTF-8, and it is Python 3 source's default. Operating-system files and C strings are not universally UTF-8, and decoding defaults depend on the interface and configuration.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> The previous website-adoption percentage is omitted: it lacked a dated survey and sampling definition, so it was not reliable evidence for a current universal figure.

## Key takeaways
- UTF-8 uses one to four bytes per scalar value.
- Continuation bytes begin with the bits 10.
- Only shortest valid forms are permitted.

## Further reading
- [Unicode 17 conformance and encoding forms](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode17.0.0/core-spec/chapter-3/)
- [RFC 3629: UTF-8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629)

questions.prompt: How many bytes does UTF-8 use to encode `é` (U+00E9)?

options.explanation: Only U+0000 to U+007F (ASCII) fit in one byte. 0xE9 = 233 is above 127.
Correct. U+0080 to U+07FF use two bytes: `110xxxxx 10xxxxxx`. é is `C3 A9`.
Three-byte encodings cover scalar values U+0800–FFFF, excluding the surrogate range, such as € (U+20AC).
Four-byte UTF-8 encodes supplementary scalar values above U+FFFF, including many emoji (some emoji are in the BMP).

questions.workedExample: U+00E9 lies above ASCII and within the two-byte UTF-8 range, so it takes two bytes. It encodes as `C3 A9`. Latin-1 instead uses the single byte `E9`, showing why knowing a code point is not enough to interpret an arbitrary byte sequence.

questions.prompt: You start reading a valid UTF-8 stream in the middle. Which of these bytes **cannot** be the first byte of a character?

options.explanation: `0100 0001` starts with 0: a complete one-byte (ASCII) character, 'A'.
`1100 0011` starts with `110`: the lead byte of a two-byte sequence.
`1110 0010` starts with `1110`: the lead byte of a three-byte sequence.
Correct. `1001 1111` starts with `10`, which marks a continuation byte. Skip forward until a byte that does not start with `10`.

questions.workedExample:
Look at the top bits of each byte:

| Byte | Bits | Role |
|---|---|---|
| 41 | 0100 0001 | ASCII |
| C3 | 1100 0011 | 2-byte lead |
| E2 | 1110 0010 | 3-byte lead |
| 9F | 1001 1111 | continuation |

Any byte from 0x80 to 0xBF is a continuation byte. This property, **self-synchronisation**, means a decoder that lands mid-character skips at most 3 bytes.

questions.prompt: A Latin-1 file stores ñ as the single byte `F1`. A program relabels that file UTF-8 without converting its bytes. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing: code-point numbers are always the same bytes
options.explanation: An encoding maps scalar values into bytes; the mappings differ.

options.text: A byte above the ASCII range cannot by itself be a complete UTF-8 scalar-value encoding
options.explanation: Correct. The Latin-1 byte must be decoded and then re-encoded into the appropriate UTF-8 sequence.

options.text: UTF-8 represents every non-ASCII scalar in four bytes
options.explanation: UTF-8 uses two, three or four bytes for non-ASCII scalar values, depending on the value.

options.text: The only missing step is reversing the file's bytes
options.explanation: UTF-8 has no endian variant; this is an encoding mismatch.

questions.workedExample: Separate the original byte from the intended scalar value. Latin-1 maps `F1` directly to ñ. UTF-8 encodes that scalar as `C3 B1`; changing a label does not perform that conversion.

questions.prompt: A valid UTF-8 sequence starts with `1110` and has two continuation bytes. Why can the three bytes not simply be concatenated as a code-point number?

options.text: Every sequence must be reversed first
options.explanation: UTF-8 byte order is already specified and is not reversed by host endianness.

options.text: The prefix bits mark the sequence structure and are not payload
options.explanation: Correct. Decode the payload positions after removing the lead and continuation markers.

options.text: Only the last byte carries data
options.explanation: All three bytes carry some code-point payload bits.

options.text: Three-byte UTF-8 is always invalid
options.explanation: Three-byte sequences encode many BMP scalar values, with validity restrictions.

questions.workedExample: The lead prefix identifies a three-byte sequence, and each continuation prefix marks a following byte. Only the remaining payload bits form the scalar value. A real decoder must also reject forbidden values and non-shortest forms.

questions.prompt: Which statements about UTF-8 are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every valid ASCII file is also a valid UTF-8 file with the same meaning
options.explanation: Correct. U+0000–007F encode as the identical single bytes.

options.text: In valid UTF-8, each byte can be classified as starting a scalar-value encoding or continuing one
options.explanation: Correct. Continuation bytes always begin with `10`; lead bytes never do.

options.text: Every character takes exactly two bytes
options.explanation: That is closer to UCS-2. UTF-8 is variable length: 1 to 4 bytes.

options.text: A byte order mark is required to tell little-endian from big-endian UTF-8
options.explanation: UTF-8 is a byte sequence, so it has no byte order. A UTF-8 BOM (`EF BB BF`) exists but is optional and often discouraged.

options.text: The byte 0x00 appears only when encoding U+0000
options.explanation: Correct. All bytes of multibyte sequences have the high bit set. A U+0000 inside text still terminates a C string, so arbitrary Unicode text needs explicit length handling.

questions.workedExample:
Check each against the byte table:

```
0xxxxxxx               ASCII
110xxxxx 10xxxxxx
1110xxxx 10xxxxxx ...
11110xxx 10xxxxxx ...
```

1. ASCII rows are unchanged: true.
2. `10` prefix marks continuations: true.
3. Lengths vary from 1 to 4: false.
4. Bytes have no endianness: false.
5. Every byte in a multi-byte sequence is ≥ 0x80: true.

lessons.title: UTF-16 units and surrogate pairs
lessons.summary: Supplementary scalar values use a high/low surrogate pair.
lessons.body:
A UTF-16 code unit is not always a complete code point. Supplementary scalar values need a pair whose two halves have distinct roles.

## UTF-16 and surrogate pairs

**UTF-16** uses 16-bit **code units**. BMP scalar values (excluding D800–DFFF) take one unit. Code points above U+FFFF take two, called a **surrogate pair**, built from a range of the BMP (U+D800 to U+DFFF) reserved so that no character uses it.

To encode a code point above U+FFFF:

1. Subtract 0x10000, leaving a 20-bit number.
2. The top 10 bits plus 0xD800 give the **high surrogate**.
3. The low 10 bits plus 0xDC00 give the **low surrogate**.

As a formula:

```formula reference
v = c − 0x10000
H = 0xD800 + ⌊v / 0x400⌋
L = 0xDC00 + (v mod 0x400)
where
c: the code point, from 0x10000 up to 0x10FFFF
v: c minus 0x10000, a 20-bit number from 0 to 0xFFFFF
H: the high surrogate code unit, 0xD800 to 0xDBFF: 0xD800 plus the top 10 bits of v
L: the low surrogate code unit, 0xDC00 to 0xDFFF: 0xDC00 plus the low 10 bits of v
0x400: 1,024, which is 2 to the power 10
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number; dividing by 0x400 and rounding down keeps the top 10 bits
mod: modulo, the remainder after division; v mod 0x400 is the low 10 bits
In words: split the 20-bit offset into a top half and a bottom half of 10 bits each, and add each half to the start of its reserved surrogate range.
```

The high surrogate always comes first and belongs to D800–DBFF; the low surrogate follows and belongs to DC00–DFFF. A lone half is not a complete, well-formed encoding of a supplementary scalar value.

For example, 😀 in UTF-16 is `D83D DE00`. Because of the reserved surrogate block, those 2,048 values can never be characters, leaving 1,112,064 valid **scalar values**.

UTF-16 extends an earlier 16-bit design with surrogate pairs. Java, JavaScript, Windows W APIs, .NET and Qt use 16-bit code units in their string interfaces; their adoption histories differ, so they cannot all be described as pre-1996 adopters. UTF-16 also has byte-order variants (UTF-16LE and UTF-16BE), often signalled by a **byte order mark** (BOM), U+FEFF, at the start of the file.

## Key takeaways
- Supplementary scalar values use a high/low surrogate pair.
- UTF-16 serialisation needs a byte-order convention.

## Further reading
- [Unicode 17 conformance and encoding forms](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode17.0.0/core-spec/chapter-3/)
- [RFC 3629: UTF-8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629)

questions.prompt: A UTF-16 string contains a supplementary scalar value as a high surrogate followed by a low surrogate. A slice keeps only the high surrogate. What remains?

options.text: A lone surrogate, not a well-formed encoding of that scalar value
options.explanation: Correct. Both units are needed; the retained half is not itself a Unicode scalar value.

options.text: The same complete character in fewer bytes
options.explanation: Slicing has lost part of the encoding.

options.text: A valid UTF-32 value
options.explanation: Removing a unit does not convert UTF-16 to UTF-32.

options.text: A valid pair in little-endian order
options.explanation: Endianness changes byte order within units, not the requirement for both units.

questions.workedExample: A surrogate pair divides one supplementary scalar value between two ordered code units. Keeping only one loses information. Some language string types permit lone surrogates internally, but interchange as well-formed UTF-16 requires valid pairing.

lessons.title: Bytes, code points and grapheme clusters
lessons.summary: String length depends on the unit a language counts.
lessons.body:
Before enforcing a text limit, decide what it counts: storage bytes, code units, code points or user-perceived characters.

## What is the length of a string?

There are at least four answers, and languages disagree on which one `len` returns.

```
string: "é😀"
code points        2
UTF-16 code units  3   (1 + 2)
UTF-8 bytes        6   (2 + 4)
```

| Language | `len` / `length` counts |
|---|---|
| Python 3 `str` | code points |
| JavaScript, Java | UTF-16 code units |
| Go string len; Rust str.len() | bytes (Rust str is valid UTF-8; Go strings may hold arbitrary bytes) |
| C strlen | bytes before the first NUL, regardless of encoding |

In JavaScript `'😀'.length` is 2, and slicing it in the middle can produce a lone surrogate: allowed in a JavaScript string but not well-formed UTF-16 for interchange. In C, strlen("é") is 2 if the execution string literal encoding is UTF-8; source-file encoding alone does not guarantee that.

### Graphemes: what the user sees

Even code points are not "characters" as a reader sees them. An extended **grapheme cluster** approximates a user-perceived character under Unicode segmentation rules, and it can be many code points:

- `é` can be one code point (U+00E9) or two: `e` + U+0301 COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT.
- 👍🏽 is U+1F44D plus a skin-tone modifier, U+1F3FD: 2 code points, 8 UTF-8 bytes.
- 🇬🇧 is two "regional indicator" code points, G and B.
- Family emoji join several people with U+200D ZERO WIDTH JOINER and can exceed 20 bytes.

User-facing cursor movement and character limits often need grapheme segmentation. Storage/protocol limits still need byte counts; neither replaces the other. Python's standard library has no grapheme function; the third-party `regex` module's `\X` pattern finds them.

## Key takeaways
- String length depends on the unit a language counts.
- User-perceived characters can contain several code points.

## Further reading

lessons.title: Canonical equivalence and normalisation
lessons.summary: Visually identical strings can have different code-point sequences.
lessons.body:
Text can have different code-point spellings that represent the same abstract text. Normalisation supplies a consistent spelling when that equivalence is intended.

## Normalisation

Because `é` has two spellings, two strings can look identical but compare unequal:

```python
# Compose canonically equivalent text.
import unicodedata as ud

a = 'café'      # precomposed
b = 'café'     # e + combining
a == b               # False
len(a), len(b)       # (4, 5)
ud.normalize('NFC', b) == a   # True
```

Unicode defines normal forms. **NFC** composes where possible (the usual choice for storage and comparison). **NFD** decomposes. HFS+ historically uses a modified decomposed form; other macOS file systems have different storage and comparison rules. Do not assume that all macOS filenames are byte-for-byte standard NFD. **NFKC** also folds "compatibility" variants such as `ﬁ` (one ligature code point) into `fi`, which is useful for search and usernames.

Python's `.upper()` changes letter case without performing Unicode normalisation. The two displayed spellings therefore still compare unequal after both are upper-cased; their UTF-8 byte sequences also remain different until an appropriate normal form reconciles them.

### Choose the equivalence you actually need

Canonical normalisation reconciles alternative encodings of the same abstract text. It does not make every pair of visually similar strings equal: a Latin letter and a lookalike Cyrillic letter can remain different. Font choice can also hide differences that normalisation does not remove.

Compatibility normalisation goes further. The ligature ﬁ and the two letters fi are compatibility-equivalent, so NFKC can make them match; NFC preserves their difference. That transformation can discard distinctions useful in the original text. Choose it deliberately for a search index or an identifier policy, and keep an original copy where fidelity matters.

Normalisation is also separate from case folding, language-aware sorting and path validation. Apply the rules required by the relevant protocol in a defined order. A stored normal form can simplify comparisons, but it does not make a username safe or prove two users intended the same name.

## Key takeaways
- Visually identical strings can have different code-point sequences.
- Choose a normal form according to the application and protocol.

## Further reading
- [Unicode 17 conformance and encoding forms](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode17.0.0/core-spec/chapter-3/)
- [RFC 3629: UTF-8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629)

questions.prompt: Given `a = 'caf\u00e9'` and `b = 'cafe\u0301'` in Python 3, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: `a == b` is `False`
options.explanation: Correct. They render identically, but `==` compares code points, and the sequences differ.

options.text: `len(a)` is 4 and `len(b)` is 5
options.explanation: Correct. `b` uses `e` plus U+0301 COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT, two code points for one visible character.

options.text: `unicodedata.normalize('NFC', b) == a` is `True`
options.explanation: Correct. NFC composes `e` + U+0301 into the precomposed U+00E9.

options.text: `a.encode('utf-8') == b.encode('utf-8')` is `True`
options.explanation: Encoding preserves the code point difference: `a` ends `C3 A9`, `b` ends `65 CC 81`.

options.text: `a.upper() == b.upper()` is `True`
options.explanation: These uppercase results still differ: precomposed É versus E plus U+0301. Case mapping is not normalisation; in general Unicode case mappings can be context-sensitive or expand one code point into several.

questions.workedExample:
Write out the code points:

```
a: c a f é          (é = U+00E9)
b: c a f e  ́        (U+0301)
```

1. Different sequences → `a == b` is False.
2. Lengths 4 and 5.
3. NFC composes b into a → True.
4. UTF-8: `63 61 66 c3 a9` vs `63 61 66 65 cc 81` → False.
5. Case mapping does not normalise → False.

If canonical-equivalence matching is intended, normalise both strings consistently, often to NFC. Preserve original text or follow protocol-specific rules where exact bytes matter.

lessons.title: Wrong decoders and text boundary failures
lessons.summary: Declare and enforce the encoding at each boundary.
lessons.body:
Text corruption often begins at a boundary where bytes are decoded under the wrong rules. Preserve the encoding contract when storing, transmitting and validating text.

## Mojibake and other failures

### Wrong decoder

Decoding UTF-8 bytes as Windows-1252 often produces mojibake, but some bytes are undefined in strict Windows-1252 decoders and can raise errors:

```python
# A wrong decoder garbles valid bytes.
'é'.encode('utf-8').decode('cp1252')
# 'Ã©'
'€'.encode('utf-8').decode('cp1252')
# 'â‚¬'
```

Sequences such as `Ã©` or `â€™` often indicate UTF-8 decoded as Windows-1252 (though the displayed text alone is not conclusive). The fix is to know the encoding at every boundary: HTTP `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`, `open(path, encoding='utf-8')` in Python, the connection charset in a database driver.

> [!warning] MySQL's utf8 is not UTF-8
> In MySQL, the character set historically named `utf8` is really `utf8mb3`: at most 3 bytes per character, so it cannot store supplementary characters such as 😀. Some emoji are BMP characters and do fit. Inserting 😀 fails or truncates. Use `utf8mb4`, which is the default since MySQL 8.0.

### Overlong encodings

Nothing in the bit layout stops you writing `/` (U+002F) in two bytes as `C0 AF`. The standard forbids such **overlong** forms, but early decoders accepted them. Microsoft IIS was hit by a famous directory-traversal attack in 2000: `..%c0%af..` slipped past a check for `../` and was decoded to it afterwards. Correct decoders reject overlongs, lone surrogates and values above U+10FFFF. Decode strictly, apply the protocol's canonicalisation rules, then validate the decoded path and enforce containment in the intended directory. Unicode normalisation alone is not a path-traversal defence.

### Bytes versus text

Python 3 makes the distinction a type: `bytes` is raw data, `str` is a sequence of code points. You convert explicitly with `.encode()` and `.decode()`. Many Python 2 bugs came from mixing them silently. In C, `char` is a byte; functions such as toupper operate on unsigned-char values (or EOF) according to the C locale, not arbitrary Unicode characters. Passing a negative signed char value other than EOF is undefined behaviour. Processing UTF-8 byte by byte this way is not Unicode case conversion and may leave bytes unchanged or corrupt them, depending on the locale.

Case conversion is itself language-dependent: `'Straße'.upper()` is `'STRASSE'`, which is one character longer, and Turkish has a dotted and a dotless i.

## Key takeaways
- Declare and enforce the encoding at each boundary.
- Strict decoding and path containment are separate requirements.
- Byte-oriented case conversion is not Unicode case conversion.

## Further reading
- [Unicode 17 conformance and encoding forms](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode17.0.0/core-spec/chapter-3/)
- [RFC 3629: UTF-8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629)
- [UTF-8 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8)
- [UTF-16 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-16)
- [The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Must Know About Unicode — Joel Spolsky](https://www.joelonsoftware.com/2003/10/08/the-absolute-minimum-every-software-developer-absolutely-positively-must-know-about-unicode-and-character-sets-no-excuses/)
- [Unicode HOWTO — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/unicode.html)
- [RFC 3629: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629)
- [Unicode Normalization Forms (UAX #15)](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr15/)

lessons.title: Values and their byte order
lessons.summary: Endianness orders bytes of a multibyte representation.
lessons.body:
The previous lessons decided what bits mean. This one is about where they sit. In the common byte-addressed model used here (eight bits per byte), memory is an array of bytes, each with its own address, but most values are wider than a byte. A 32-bit integer occupies four consecutive addresses, which raises three questions:

1. In what **order** do its four bytes go? (Endianness.)
2. At which **addresses** may it start? (Alignment.)
3. When several values are grouped in a struct, what **gaps** does the compiler leave? (Padding.)

None of this is visible when your code does ordinary arithmetic. All of it becomes visible the moment you read raw bytes: a network packet, a binary file, a memory dump, or one type reinterpreted as another.

## Endianness

Take the 32-bit value `0x12345678`, stored at address 100. The **most significant byte** is `0x12`; the **least significant** is `0x78`.

```
address:        100  101  102  103
big-endian:      12   34   56   78
little-endian:   78   56   34   12
```

- **Big-endian** stores the most significant byte at the lowest address, the way we write numbers.
- **Little-endian** stores the least significant byte first.

The names come from *Gulliver's Travels*, where two nations go to war over which end of a boiled egg to crack. Danny Cohen borrowed them in a 1980 note, "On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace", because the choice is about as arbitrary.

### Who uses which

| Little-endian | Big-endian |
|---|---|
| x86, x86-64 | TCP/IP multi-byte header fields |
| ARM (in practice) | IBM z/Architecture |
| Common RISC-V systems (ISA also defines other modes) | PNG integers, JPEG marker-segment lengths |
| Windows bitmap (.bmp) and ZIP fields specified little-endian | Java class-file multibyte items |

ARM, PowerPC and MIPS are **bi-endian** (configurable), common Android, iOS and macOS ARM systems use little-endian data. Linux also supports big-endian ARM configurations. Network and file formats specify byte order per format; not every protocol is big-endian.

One convenient property of little-endian layouts is that the low byte is always at the same address whatever the width, so reading a 64-bit value as 32 or 8 bits needs no address adjustment, and multi-word addition can start at the lowest address. Big-endian byte dumps follow the usual written order of a multibyte hexadecimal number. Neither observation proves an overall performance advantage.

### When endianness matters

It does **not** matter for arithmetic, shifts or masks inside a program. For a uint32_t value, `x >> 24` gives its most significant octet regardless of byte order, because shifts are defined on values, not on memory.

It matters whenever bytes cross a boundary:

```c
/* Inspect the representation through */
/* bytes. */
uint32_t v = 0x12345678;
unsigned char *p = (unsigned char *)&v;
printf("%02x\n", (unsigned)p[0]);
/* 78 little-endian; 12 big-endian */
```

## Key takeaways
- Endianness orders bytes of a multibyte representation.
- Arithmetic shifts operate on values independently of memory byte order.

## Further reading
- [Linux unaligned-memory documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/unaligned-memory-access.html)
- [Python struct documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)

lessons.title: Network order and explicit byte assembly
lessons.summary: Convert protocol fields at the host/wire boundary.
lessons.body:
A protocol fixes the order of bytes on the wire independently of the host's memory layout. Convert when crossing that boundary.

### Network byte order

TCP/IP headers are big-endian, called **network byte order**. C programs convert with `htons`/`htonl` (host to network, short/long) and `ntohs`/`ntohl`. On a big-endian host they do nothing; on little-endian they swap bytes (the compiler chooses appropriate instructions or folds a constant).

```c
/* Convert the numeric port to wire */
/* order. */
struct sockaddr_in addr;
addr.sin_port = htons(8080);
/* bytes in memory: 1F 90 */
```

Forget `htons` on a little-endian machine and the bytes go out as `90 1F`, so the server listens on port 0x901F = 36,895 instead of 8,080.

In Python, `struct` and `int.to_bytes` make byte order explicit:

```python
# Pack values with an explicit byte order.
import struct
struct.pack('<I', 0x12345678).hex()
# '78563412'  (< = little-endian)
struct.pack('>I', 0x12345678).hex()
# '12345678'  (> = big-endian)
struct.pack('!H', 8080).hex()
# '1f90'      (! = network order)

int.from_bytes(b'\x01\x00\x00\x00',
               'little')   # 1
```

> [!tip] Write byte-order-independent code
> Instead of casting a buffer to `uint32_t *`, assemble the value with shifts. This works on any host and has no alignment problems. Optimising compilers often recognise this pattern; the exact instruction sequence depends on alignment support, target and optimisation settings.

```c
/* Assemble bytes as values, not */
/* pointers. */
uint32_t rd_be32(const uint8_t *b) {
    return (uint32_t)b[0] << 24 |
           (uint32_t)b[1] << 16 |
           (uint32_t)b[2] << 8  |
           (uint32_t)b[3];
}
```

File formats either fix an order (PNG is big-endian; Windows bitmap images, ZIP and most Windows formats are little-endian) or record it. TIFF files start with `II` (Intel, little) or `MM` (Motorola, big). UTF-16 can use a byte order mark or an externally specified byte-order convention; a BOM is not universally required.

## Key takeaways
- Convert protocol fields at the host/wire boundary.
- Byte-by-byte assembly avoids a misaligned typed pointer.

## Further reading
- [Linux unaligned-memory documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/unaligned-memory-access.html)
- [Python struct documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)

lessons.title: Natural alignment and unaligned accesses
lessons.summary: Natural alignment is a divisibility condition on an address.
lessons.body:
An address can hold the right bytes and still be unsuitable for a typed access. Alignment connects language requirements, ABI layout and hardware behaviour.

## Alignment

A value is **naturally aligned** if its address is a whole multiple of its own size.

Natural alignment puts a four-byte value at 0, 4, 8 and so on, and an eight-byte value at multiples of eight. A type's actual required alignment comes from the ABI and can differ from its size. For these power-of-two sizes, alignment also has a bit test: an address is a multiple of 8 exactly when its low 3 bits are 0.

### Why hardware cares

A CPU can issue byte-sized loads. Cacheable misses commonly transfer whole cache lines, often 64 bytes, while individual load and store instructions, and uncached or device accesses, have additional size and alignment rules.

```
cache line boundary at 64
          ...60 61 62 63|64 65 66 67...
aligned int at 60:  [==========]
misaligned at 62:         [====|====]
                         spans 2 lines
```

When a power-of-two access size is no larger than and divides the line/page size, natural alignment keeps that access within a boundary. This does not mean every aligned object, arbitrarily wide access or generated instruction requires only one memory transaction. A misaligned one may need two accesses, two cache lines, even two page translations. The consequences depend on the architecture:

- **x86** handles many ordinary misaligned loads in hardware; alignment-requiring instruction forms and alignment-checking modes can fault. Within a cache line, ordinary unaligned loads can have little or no extra cost on many modern x86 processors. Crossing a line or page can add work; the actual penalty depends on the instruction, processor and cache/TLB state. A misaligned `lock`-prefixed atomic that spans two cache lines (a **split lock**) stalls the whole memory system, and recent Linux kernels can warn about or penalise processes that do it.
- **ARMv8 (AArch64)** handles most misaligned ordinary loads and stores in hardware, but its exclusive and atomic instructions generally require aligned addresses and fault otherwise.
- **Strict-alignment targets**, including relevant older ARM, SPARC and microcontroller configurations, can fault on unsupported unaligned accesses. Linux may emulate an access or report a signal such as SIGBUS; some hardware instead performs an unintended access, so consult the target rules.
- **Atomicity** depends on the architecture, memory type and access. For example, x86-64 guarantees indivisibility for suitably aligned ordinary 8-byte loads/stores to ordinary write-back memory. A misaligned access can lack that guarantee. In C/C++, hardware non-tearing does not permit data races: use atomics or synchronisation for conflicting cross-thread accesses.

In C, conversion to an object-pointer type with unmet alignment requirements is already undefined, and dereferencing misaligned storage is not made valid by the hardware, even on x86, and compilers vectorise code on the assumption that it does not happen. Use memcpy into a suitably typed local variable for unaligned representation copies, with valid bounds and a valid destination representation; byte order still needs handling. Compilers can lower fixed-size copies to ordinary loads where the target allows them.

## Key takeaways
- Natural alignment is a divisibility condition on an address.
- Hardware tolerance does not make a misaligned C pointer valid.
- Non-tearing hardware access does not permit a C data race.

## Further reading
- [Linux unaligned-memory documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/unaligned-memory-access.html)
- [Python struct documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)

questions.prompt: A target tolerates an unaligned load in hardware. Does that make it valid C to convert a byte-buffer address to an inadequately aligned `int *` and use it?

options.text: Yes, hardware behaviour defines every C pointer operation
options.explanation: The compiler also relies on the C type's alignment requirements.

options.text: Yes, provided the value would fit in int
options.explanation: Representability does not repair the pointer alignment.

options.text: Only if the bytes use little-endian order
options.explanation: Byte order and alignment are separate constraints.

options.text: No; copy valid bytes into a suitably aligned local value instead
options.explanation: Correct. Hardware tolerance does not satisfy the language's typed-pointer alignment requirement.

questions.workedExample: Separate the machine's load support from the language contract. An inadequately aligned conversion is already undefined in C. A bounded `memcpy` into an aligned local can avoid that typed access, provided the bytes form a valid destination representation; byte order still needs handling.

lessons.title: Struct member offsets and tail padding
lessons.summary: The ABI determines member alignment and struct layout.
lessons.body:
A struct's size includes the space needed to keep its members and array elements aligned. That size can exceed the sum of its field sizes.

## Struct padding

A C compiler lays out struct members **in declaration order** (it may not reorder them) and inserts **padding** so that each member is aligned. For ordinary unpacked structs without bit-fields, explicit over-alignment or unusual members, mainstream ABIs such as x86-64 System V and AArch64 use these rules:

1. Each member starts at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment.
2. The struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members.
3. The struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment (**tail padding**).

### Worked example

```c
/* ABI alignment leaves gaps between */
/* fields. */
struct A {
    char a;   /* 1 byte  */
    int  b;   /* 4 bytes */
    char c;   /* 1 byte  */
};
```

Lay it out byte by byte:

```
offset 0     a
offset 1-3   padding (b needs 4)
offset 4-7   b
offset 8     c
offset 9-11  tail padding
sizeof = 12, alignment 4
```

Each member moves forward to the next offset satisfying its alignment. The final size is rounded up to the struct's alignment too.

Six bytes of data, six bytes of padding. Why the tail padding? In an array `struct A arr[2]`, `arr[1]` starts sizeof(struct A) **bytes** after arr[0], namely `(unsigned char *)arr + sizeof(struct A)`. The expression `arr + sizeof(struct A)` would incorrectly scale that count by the element size again. If the size were 9, `arr[1].b` would sit at offset 13, misaligned. Rounding the size to 12 keeps every element aligned.

Reorder the members largest first and the padding mostly vanishes:

```c
/* Place the widest member first. */
struct B {
    int  b;   /* offset 0 */
    char a;   /* offset 4 */
    char c;   /* offset 5 */
};            /* sizeof = 8 */
```

With 8-byte members the effect is larger:

| Struct | Layout | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `{char; double; char}` | 1+7+8+1+7 | 24 |
| `{double; char; char}` | 8+1+1+6 | 16 |

For an array of ten million of them, that is 240 MB against 160 MB, and more of the useful data fits in each cache line. Tools such as `pahole` (from the `dwarves` package) print a struct's layout with every hole, and Clang's `-Wpadded` warns about padding.

You can always check the compiler's decisions:

```c
/* Inspect size, member offset / */
/* alignment. */
#include <stddef.h>
printf("%zu %zu %zu\n",
       sizeof(struct A),
       offsetof(struct A, c),
       _Alignof(struct A));
/* 12 8 4 */
```

> [!note] ABI-dependent
> Alignment of each type comes from the platform ABI, not the C standard. On 32-bit x86 Linux (i386 System V), a `double` inside a struct is only 4-byte aligned, so `{char; double; char}` is 16 bytes there, not 24. Code that shares binary structs between platforms cannot rely on the layout.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Marked parking bays
> Vehicles must begin at designated bay markings, so empty space may remain between them.
>
> **How it maps:** Member alignment restricts starting offsets. Tail padding makes the next struct in an array start at a suitable boundary too.
>
> **Where it stops:** The ABI determines exact byte layout; compilers do not rearrange ordinary C members to find a better fit.

## Key takeaways
- The ABI determines member alignment and struct layout.
- Tail padding preserves alignment in an array.
- Reordering members can reduce wasted space.

## Further reading
- [Linux unaligned-memory documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/unaligned-memory-access.html)
- [Python struct documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)

questions.prompt: An ordinary ABI gives a struct four-byte alignment. Its last member ends after byte offset 8, yet `sizeof` is 12. What is the purpose of the final three bytes?

options.text: They store hidden copies of the fields
options.explanation: Padding is not duplicate field storage.

options.text: They encode the struct's byte order
options.explanation: The ABI's endian rule is separate from padding.

options.text: They keep the next array element correctly aligned
options.explanation: Correct. Array stride is sizeof the element, so tail padding preserves alignment.

options.text: They allow the compiler to reorder declared members
options.explanation: Ordinary C members retain declaration order.

questions.workedExample: The next array element begins one complete struct size after the current one. A stride of nine would misalign later elements. Rounding the size up to twelve preserves four-byte alignment even though the last three bytes hold no declared member.

questions.prompt: A private struct has small fields separated by highly aligned fields. You want to reduce its array footprint without weakening member alignment. Which is the best first investigation?

options.text: Remove every gap with a packed attribute
options.explanation: Packing may create misaligned members and change access requirements.

options.text: Reorder members and inspect the resulting ABI layout
options.explanation: Correct. Grouping fields can reduce padding while keeping each field aligned.

options.text: Assume sizeof is always the sum of field sizes
options.explanation: That ignores member and tail padding.

options.text: Change only the array's starting alignment
options.explanation: That does not remove padding inside each element or change its stride.

questions.workedExample: Inspect the current member offsets and gaps. Reordering can let smaller fields share space that would otherwise be padding, while the ABI still aligns every member. Check sizeof and offsets after the change, and do not silently change a layout shared with external consumers.

questions.prompt: The next unused offset in a struct is five, but the next member requires four-byte alignment. Why must the compiler leave a gap before that member?

options.text: It can move earlier declared fields behind the new member
options.explanation: Ordinary C member order is fixed by the declaration.

options.text: Every field must start at an odd offset
options.explanation: Alignment is a multiple requirement, not an odd-offset rule.

options.text: The member's size alone guarantees alignment
options.explanation: The member's starting address must satisfy its alignment too.

options.text: Offset five does not meet the member's alignment requirement
options.explanation: Correct. The compiler advances to the next suitable offset, eight in this example.

questions.workedExample: A member begins at an address satisfying its ABI alignment. The next free byte can fail that rule, so padding advances the member to a permitted starting position. The gap preserves valid access; it is not additional user data.

lessons.title: Packed members and representation leaks
lessons.summary: Packed layout can create misaligned members.
lessons.body:
Removing padding changes alignment obligations, while copying padding can expose data you never intended to send. Internal layout needs care at external boundaries.

### Packed structs

`__attribute__((packed))` (GCC/Clang) or `#pragma pack(1)` (also MSVC) reduces padding. With the earlier four-byte-int ABI, a simple char-int-char struct becomes six bytes. Nested types and explicit alignment constraints can still retain padding; inspect the actual layout. This is used to match an exact wire or file format. The costs:

- Members may be misaligned, so the compiler must use slower byte-by-byte or unaligned access sequences on some targets.
- Taking a pointer to a packed member (`&p->b`) can produce a misaligned int pointer. Using it can fault or otherwise misbehave; GCC warns with `-Waddress-of-packed-member`.
- Atomic operations on packed members may be impossible or not atomic.

Reordering members is almost always a better first step than packing.

## Bugs and security holes

### Padding leaks data

Assigning a struct's fields does not guarantee defined values for its padding. Copying its entire object representation can therefore disclose stale bytes, which might be part of a key, a pointer (defeating ASLR) or another user's data. Implementation-specific fixes may zero storage before filling it. Portable C still permits padding to take unspecified values when a struct or member is stored, so a blanket memset-then-fill recipe is not a universal guarantee. Serialise the intended fields into an explicitly defined output buffer, including explicit zero bytes where the format requires them.

The same padding makes `memcmp(&x, &y, sizeof x)` unreliable for equality: two structs with equal members can differ in their padding bytes. Compare members individually.

### Raw structs are not a file format

`fwrite(&s, sizeof s, 1, f)` on one machine and `fread` on another breaks as soon as the two differ in endianness, padding, type sizes (`long` is 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux, 4 on 64-bit Windows) or compiler flags. Use an explicit format: fixed-width types written field by field in a stated byte order, or a serialisation library such as Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto, which specify their byte layouts exactly.

## Key takeaways
- Packed layout can create misaligned members.
- Padding can leak information and defeats raw-byte equality checks.
- Serialise fields using an explicit external format.

## Further reading
- [Linux unaligned-memory documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/unaligned-memory-access.html)
- [Python struct documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)

questions.prompt: An x86-64 Linux kernel driver fills a `struct info { char flags; long id; }` on the stack, sets both fields, and copies the whole struct to user space with `copy_to_user`. A security review flags it as an information leak. Why?

options.text: `long` has a different size in user space
options.explanation: On a given 64-bit Linux ABI, kernel and user `long` are both 8 bytes. Compat layers aside, that is not the leak.

options.text: Seven bytes of padding can retain or acquire unspecified data; copying the entire object can disclose it
options.explanation: Correct. Field assignments do not guarantee padding bytes. Explicitly encode fields in a defined output layout; a source-level memset followed by stores is not a universal portable-C padding guarantee.

options.text: `copy_to_user` copies the struct in big-endian order
options.explanation: `copy_to_user` copies raw bytes in order; it does no byte swapping, and byte order is not a confidentiality issue.

options.text: Stack memory is always readable from user space
options.explanation: Kernel stack memory is not mapped into user space. The leak happens only because the driver explicitly copies uninitialised bytes out.

questions.workedExample:
1. Under the stated ABI, flags is at offset 0 and id at 8, leaving seven padding bytes.
2. Assigning fields does not specify their values.
3. Copying the whole representation can leak stale information.
4. Encode the intended fields into a fully initialised output buffer; do not rely on portable C to preserve zero padding after subsequent member stores. Implementation-specific zeroing fixes require checking the compiler and generated code.

options.text: `len` is at offset 1, so `p` is a misaligned `uint32_t *`; the compiler emits a normal 4-byte load through it, which faults
options.explanation: Correct. Direct `h->len` access is compiled with byte-safe loads because the compiler knows the member is packed. Through a plain pointer that knowledge is lost.

options.text: Packed structs are stored big-endian
options.explanation: Packing changes padding, not byte order. Endianness would give a wrong value, not a fault.

options.text: `h` itself must be on the heap
options.explanation: Where the struct lives does not matter. The problem is the alignment of the address being loaded from.

options.text: `uint32_t` cannot be packed
options.explanation: The compiler extension allows this integer member in a packed struct. A plain pointer can lose the compiler's knowledge of reduced member alignment.

questions.workedExample:
1. With eight-bit bytes and the stated compiler extension, packed layout: `type` at 0, `len` at 1–4. sizeof = 5.
2. If `h` is 4-byte aligned, the member address is `(unsigned char *)h + 1`, not a multiple of 4. Plain h + 1 advances by sizeof *h, not one byte.
3. `h->len`: the compiler knows the field may be misaligned and emits byte loads plus shifts.
4. `*p`: `p` is an ordinary `uint32_t *`, assumed aligned, so the compiler may emit an alignment-requiring load. That explains the stipulated fault; the exact instruction sequence depends on compilation.

GCC warns with `-Waddress-of-packed-member`. Safer: `uint32_t v; memcpy(&v, (const unsigned char *)h + 1, sizeof v);`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about alignment are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: On x86, a `lock`-prefixed atomic on data that spans two cache lines (a split lock) is far slower than an aligned one and can stall other cores
options.explanation: Correct. The CPU has to lock the bus or equivalent to keep the operation atomic across two lines.

options.text: A suitably aligned ordinary 8-byte hardware load/store to ordinary write-back memory on x86-64 is non-tearing; C data-race rules still apply
options.explanation: Correct. Hardware atomicity of this access does not make unsynchronised conflicting accesses to a plain C object valid.

options.text: In C, dereferencing a misaligned `int *` is undefined behaviour even on x86
options.explanation: Correct. The hardware may tolerate it, but the language does not, and the optimiser (for example, the vectoriser) may assume alignment.

options.text: x86 raises a fault on every misaligned load
options.explanation: x86 handles misaligned ordinary loads in hardware, usually with little or no penalty within a cache line. Strict-alignment CPUs are the ones that fault.

options.text: `memcmp` on two structs reliably tells you whether all their members are equal
options.explanation: Padding bytes are unspecified, so two structs with equal members can differ in their padding and compare unequal.

questions.workedExample:
1. Split locks: true. Linux on recent Intel CPUs can detect them and warn about or slow down the offending process.
2. Aligned 8-byte atomicity on x86-64: true; this is why aligned `uint64_t` loads and stores need no lock to avoid tearing (though C atomics or other synchronisation are needed to avoid data races, not merely to request ordering).
3. UB in C: true; use `memcpy` for unaligned reads.
4. x86 faults: false; it tolerates misalignment (some instruction forms require alignment, and alignment-checking modes can also fault).
5. `memcmp` on structs: false because of padding.

questions.prompt: For `uint32_t x = 0x12345678;` on hosts with eight-bit bytes and 32-bit int, which operations expose different byte orders between little- and big-endian systems? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Shifts are defined on values, not memory, so this is always the most significant byte.

options.text: `((unsigned char *)&x)[0]`
options.explanation: Correct. This reads whichever byte sits at the lowest address: the least significant byte on little-endian, the most significant byte on big-endian.

options.text: `memcpy(buf, &x, 4)` then sending `buf` over a socket
options.explanation: Correct. The raw buffers have different byte sequences; what a receiver makes of them depends on its decoder.
Arithmetic works on values. The product is the same everywhere (mod 2³²).

options.text: Writing an array of `x` with `fwrite` and reading it with `fread` on the other kind of machine
options.explanation: Correct. The file stores raw memory bytes, so a big-endian reader sees every value byte-swapped.

questions.workedExample:
Endianness only shows when you look at the **bytes in memory**:

| Expression | Touches memory bytes? |
|---|---|
| `(x >> 24) & 0xFF` | no |
| `((uchar*)&x)[0]` | yes |
| `memcpy` + send | yes |
| `x * 256` | no |
| `fwrite`/`fread` | yes |

Portable code converts at the boundary with `htonl`/`ntohl`, or builds bytes with shifts, so the in-program arithmetic never needs to care.

lessons.title: Native packing and performance alignment
lessons.summary: Python native struct packing omits automatic tail padding.
lessons.body:
A library's native packing rules are not automatically identical to a C struct's complete layout. Alignment also affects performance through object spacing and access boundaries.

### Python's struct module and padding

Python's `struct` uses native alignment with the default `@` prefix, but does **not** add tail padding. On an ABI with four-byte `int` size and alignment:

```python
# Native packing omits automatic tail pads.
import struct
struct.calcsize('@cic')    # 9, not 12
struct.calcsize('@cic0i')  # 12: 0i pads
struct.calcsize('<cic')    # 6: no padding
```

The `0i` trick pads the end to an `int` boundary. Any explicit byte-order prefix (`<`, `>`, `!`, `=`) turns alignment off entirely. ctypes.Structure can model supported C ABIs with tail padding; its layout/packing options must match the actual compiler ABI and flags, so it is not a universal mirror of arbitrary structs.

## Alignment for performance

Sometimes you want **more** alignment than natural:

- **SIMD**: aligned AVX/AVX-512 load forms require their specified alignment; unaligned forms also exist. Alignment can avoid split accesses, but performance depends on the instruction and processor.
- **False sharing**: two threads updating different variables on the same 64-byte cache line force the line to bounce between CPU cores. Separate counters by the relevant cache-line size, including alignment and stride/padding. alignas(64) on the start of an array alone does not separate adjacent counters. C++17 hardware_destructive_interference_size is an implementation-provided size hint, used with alignas and an appropriate layout; speedups depend on the workload. The caches module covers why, in its lesson on coherence.
- **Pages**: mapping and device interfaces may require page or device-specific alignment. Query the page size; 4 KiB is common, not universal. aligned_alloc and posix_memalign align virtual allocations, but do not alone pin memory, ensure physical contiguity or map it for DMA; use the required operating-system device API.

## Key takeaways
- Python native struct packing omits automatic tail padding.
- Alignment, stride and object layout together affect false sharing.
- An aligned allocation alone is not a DMA mapping.

## Further reading
- [Linux unaligned-memory documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/unaligned-memory-access.html)
- [Python struct documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)
- [Endianness — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endianness)
- [Data structure alignment — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure_alignment)
- [The Lost Art of Structure Packing — Eric S. Raymond](http://www.catb.org/esr/structure-packing/)
- [struct: interpret bytes as packed binary data — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)
- [On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace (IEN 137) — Danny Cohen](https://www.rfc-editor.org/ien/ien137.txt)
- [byteorder(3) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/byteorder.3.html)

questions.prompt: On an x86-64 or AArch64 Linux/macOS ABI with four-byte int size and alignment, what does `struct.calcsize('@cic')` return in Python?

options.explanation: 6 is the unaligned size, which you get with a byte-order prefix such as `<cic` or `=cic`. `@` uses native alignment.
12 is the C `sizeof`, but Python's `struct` does not add tail padding. Append `0i` to get 12.
Correct. `c` at 0, 3 bytes padding, `i` at 4–7, `c` at 8: 9 bytes, with no tail padding.
Nothing here needs 8-byte alignment; the widest item is a 4-byte `int`.

questions.workedExample:
With `@` (the default), `struct` aligns each item as the platform's C compiler would, but stops after the last item:

```
0     c
1-3   pad
4-7   i
8     c      -> 9 bytes
```

- `'@cic0i'` → 12 (`0i` adds alignment padding but no data).
- `'<cic'` → 6 (explicit byte order turns padding off).

For exact C struct mirrors, use `ctypes.Structure`, whose `sizeof` here is 12.
